I should like to make an inquiry of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe). Representations have been made to me by certain milling interests in my constituency that on June 6 next the export rate on winter wheat flour is being increased by the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways by approximately 6 cents per barrel. They further say that Australian flour is competing very strongly with our product in the West Indies at present and that in the interests of the wheat producing farmers and millers in Ontario no further handicap should be placed upon their efforts to compete successfully in outside markets. Will the minister kindly take
[Mr. Gardiner.l

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURE TO BE MADE EFFECTIVE BY RAILWAYS ON JUNE 6
speechtext: I have no knowledge of the proposed increase in rates, but I may say that it is not the function of the minister to take up with the railways matters of rates. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES DELAY IN DELIVERY OF LOCKHEED TRANSPORT PLANES AND QUESTION OF SALES TO JAPAN
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the government, and I am sorry that I was unable to give longer notice of it. Will the government make a statement regarding the alleged delay in the delivery of aeroplanes for the Winnipeg-Toronto-Montreal service on account of the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation of Canada having accepted a contract for the delivery of thirty of their planes to the Japanese government, including several allegedly already commenced for delivery to our service; and will the government assure the house that no licence will be issued for the export of such planes to Japan?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) :
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES DELAY IN DELIVERY OF LOCKHEED TRANSPORT PLANES AND QUESTION OF SALES TO JAPAN
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend's question may I say that Canada does not manufacture planes of the standard transport type. The order for the requirements of Trans-Canada Air Lines was therefore placed in the United States, with the company that manufactures practically all the requirements in that regard for this continent. Our deliveries have been delayed, as I presume all deliveries have been delayed in connection with planes of this type. I have no knowledge that exports to Japan have anything to do with it. However, if they have, it is a matter between the government of the United States and Japan.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: PROSPECTIVE SALE TO FOREIGN INTERESTS- STRATEGIC AND DIPLOMATIC CONSIDERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to
the Montreal Star, at the annual meeting of the Consolidated Paper Corporation the president, Mr. L. J. Belnap, referred to the prospective sale of Anticosti Island to parties in Holland who several months ago had secured an option. Several months ago a group of German technicians had made a careful survey of the island, and it is suspected that this is the group that secured the option. Be that as it may, is it in the general interest that the ownership or control of this island should pass into the control of a foreign company? It would seem that important strategic and diplomatic considerations are involved.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROSPECTIVE SALE TO FOREIGN INTERESTS- STRATEGIC AND DIPLOMATIC CONSIDERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say
to the hon. member that the government is aware of the importance of the island from the point of view to which he has made reference, and different departments of the government have been making inquiries concerning the situation. I believe the interests of the country are being fully safeguarded in the matter as it stands at the present time, and the situation will continue to be watched.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Fruit and vegetable products, including grant of $5,000 to the Canadian Horticultural Council, $555,000.

Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned last night the item had been discussed at considerable length. One is struck
by the large proportion of the vote which is allotted to salaries, namely $414,000 odd.
The details of the vote indicate that there are 137 inspectors, and provision for their salaries is made in the item. While one does not desire in any way to curtail or limit reasonable and necessary expenditures for the promotion of agriculture, and while one realizes that distances are great and that there are other circumstances which must be considered, yet it would appear that this is a large number of inspectors for one branch. We hear a great deal in these days about the excessive costs of government, and we hear the charge that there is too much overlapping. In other branches of the Department of Agriculture as well there are many inspectors. Does not the minister think that the efforts of the inspectors in the different branches could be coordinated and some saving effected in this respect? Is it necessary to have this large number of inspectors in one branch? Could not their work be consolidated with that of other inspectors, or could not the inspectors in this branch take on the work of those in other branches?
Travelling expenses must be heavy, and it seems to me that to a certain extent these inspectors must be crossing and recrossing each others' trails. What provinces are undertaking the same kind of work? Is there any duplication or overlapping in the provincial and federal services? How many of the inspectors are assigned to each province, district, or whatever the division is termed? Answers to these questions are important in view of the undoubted and widespread contention that the cost of government is excessive, and that there is duplication and overlapping. I repeat that I do not wish in any way to limit the number of officials who take part in the promotion of the necessary work of the department or who are required to assist in the development of a great industry. But this is not a new subject in the house. Year after year we have heard statements about the very large number of inspectors and the amount of money expended in these services. There is a suggestion of duplication and overlapping, and there would seem to be a necessity for consolidation and economy.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the question raised by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) is a proper one. The total estimate for the branch is $555,000. The earnings of inspectors are approximately $125,000, leaving a net amount of about $430,000 voted to cover entire expenses over and above earnings.
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

There are 42 inspectors in Prince Edward Island, 43 in New Brunswick, 88 in Nova Scotia, 92 in British Columbia and 77 in western Ontario. Those are the sections in which the greater part of the fruit and vegetables are produced. Not all the inspectors are on full time; a considerable number of them are seasonal employees who work only during the season when inspections are being made and the crop is harvested.
The question whether this work can be done more cheaply by preventing overlapping through the use of inspectors from other services is one that might stand some consideration. However, I am sure it will be realized that inspectors who are inspecting fruit would be expected to be familiar with the growing, packing and marketing of fruit. I believe it has been considered by those who have been in charge of the department in days gone by that it is better to have this service performed seasonally by people who are familiar with the industry than to use inspectors who might be employed throughout the year and used for one purpose at one time and for another purpose at another. Which would be the least costly I am not prepared to say at the moment, but I am inclined to think that the best service can be obtained by using men who are familiar with tihe particular work when they are required.
As far as staff is concerned, the figures do not indicate any great increase in staff for inspection purposes. There were 14 senior fruit and vegetable inspectors last year, and the figure for this year is the same. There were 20 supervising fruit and vegetable inspectors last year, and the figure for this year is 22, an increase of two. There were three fruit and vegetable inspectors, grade 2, last year, and the number is the same this year. There were 13 fruit and vegetable inspectors, grade 1, last year, and 13 this year. There were 82 fruit and vegetable inspectors, grade 1. seasonal, last year, with the same number this year.
There is one part of the minister's answer that suggests further inquiry. What is the reason for the large number of inspectors in Prince Edward Island?
Principally because of the large production of potatoes and turnips in that province. These products are shipped either to other parts of Canada or to other countries.
Are there any inspectors in Ontario?
There are 77 in western Ontario alone.
Are any new orchards being planted in the various fruit growing areas of Canada?
There is no pronounced expansion in the planting of fruit trees at the present time, but the usual replacement planting is being carried on.
Would this vote cover inspectors at the experimental farms who deal with the diseases of vegetables and fruits?
None of this inspection is done through the experimental farms.
But there is some carried od at the experimental farms?
Only the certified seed potato inspection, and the work having to do with diseases.

I agree with the minister that this inspection service is very important to the fruit and vegetable industry. The other night the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) referred to the lack of statistics in connection with this industry. If hon. members had proper statistics before them they would appreciate the value of this production. I believe that this industry is worth $150,000,000 to the Dominion of Canada. A grant of $5,000 to the Canadian Horticultural Council is included in this vote. I believe at one time this grant was either $8,000 or $9,000. No other organization of producers covers the country so completely as this one. It is performing a great work, and I submit the minister should consider the granting of more assistance to this organization than is provided for in this item.

May I just supplement the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark) with respect to statistics in connection with the vegetable industry. I dealt with this matter the other night for a moment or two under another item, but I should like to ask the minister at this time if any move has been made recently to provide a complete picture of the entire vegetable industry. If so, could he give us the details?

The gathering of statistics of this kind is done by the bureau of statistics under the Department of Trade and Commerce. We give them all the assistance we possibly can in that regard. I do not believe there is anything of an exceptional nature under way at the present time.
In reply to the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark) I would point out that down to 1931-32 the grant to the horticultural association was $8,000. In 1932-33 the grant was reduced to $5,000, which, with the deduction of

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
ten per cent in effect at that time, made the net grant 84,500. The deduction has been restored and the grant is now $5,000. There was first a ten per cent deduction, then a five per cent deduction and it is now $5,000 even. The matter of giving further assistance has been under consideration, but we did not think it possible to increase the grant this year.

There are certain fruit growing areas in Ontario which have difficulty in marketing their production on account of the lateness of their seasons. Is there any way in which the department assists in the marketing of these fruits that come along so late?

Some assistance has been given in Ontario, particularly to those sections producing grapes and peaches. This assistance was in the form of advertising last fall when the fruit was coming on with a rush. The provincial authorities cooperated with us in that and I think it is generally recognized that good results were obtained. The fruit was got rid of in great volume and to better advantage than in previous years.
Are there any other areas in Canada that have this difficulty because of the season?
Every section of Canada has its own peculiar disadvantage in connection with fruit growing. We are so far north that our fruit comes in a little later than the fruits in the United States.
I was not referring particularly to the United States; I was interested in the districts in Canada.

That is where the
comparison is made. There is difficulty in Canada because we are so far north and our fruit comes on a little later. Sometimes there is difficulty in getting rid of a large crop, but we pay attention to all parts of Canada equally.

I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) with respect to the inspection of fruit as applying to the Niagara district, which I have the honour to represent. I am pleased to note that the minister has under consideration increasing the grant to the horticultural council, which has done splendid work. The amount of 85,000 is very small to take care of a work which is national in its scope.

As the committee knows, there are two branches of the service, the fruit and vegetable inspectors, who take *care of the inspection of table stock potatoes 51952-187
and fruit shipments and vegetables, and the plant disease investigators, who take care of seed potato inspection. I understand that these two branches of the service are being amalgamated, or are to be administered under the one head, and I should like the minister to give the committee some information as to what the lay-out will be in the future and who will be the head of the branch. I understand that the table stock and fruit and vegetable inspectors have always received higher pay than the members of the other branch of the service. But to my way of thinking a plant disease investigator has to be a very much more competent man, and the head of the service in the different provinces has to be a university graduate who has had years of training for his position. It would seem to me, therefore, that the two branches of the service should be on a par so far as remuneration is concerned.

I understand, Mr. Chairman, that there has been a reclassification of the positions concerned, but there is no bringing together of the two services. I understood the objection of my hon. friend was to an amalgamation of these services, but that is not being done. One group is provided for under this vote, and the other group under production.

I have received a number of complaints from fruit growers in the Nelson area of British Columbia against the tremendous cost of shipping their fruit into Alberta. Has the government considered subsidizing in any way the shipments of fruit from that area going into Alberta?

There is a question, of course, whether the people of the Nelson district are any further away from certain sections of Alberta than those of the Okanagan and other fruit growing districts of the province. The government has not considered bonusing the shipment of fruit from that area.

One fruit grower told me that he had shipped fruit from Nelson to New Zealand or Australia and made a little money on it, but on another shipment to Calgary he lost money because the freight was more than the value of the fruit.
That has always been the case.

While we are discussing advertising, which the minister mentioned a few moments ago in connection with the fruits and vegetables of Ontario and other provinces, may I draw his attention to the reported vote by congress during the latter part of 1937 of

Supply-Agriculture-M arketing

$2,000,000 for the fruit and vegetable industry and other branches of agriculture in the United States, which I think may have its effects upon Canada so far as the marketing of their products in this country is concerned.
We have been experiencing, as the minister well knows, a great influx of citrus fruits from the United States during the last decade and longer. No matter what we may hear with respect to the matter, I have no doubt at all that these imported citrus fruits do displace some of our home grown fresh fruits. It is very difficult to understand any reasoning to the contrary. We permit the importation of oranges and other types of citrus fruits, and while our consuming population must have them, at the same time I think we should meet that competition by a well-organized advertising campaign in favour of our own fresh fruits and vegetables. I should like the government to give its earnest consideration to a new type of advertising for our fresh fruits and fresh vegetables. There is nothing better in the whole world, from the standpoint either of health or of delieiousness, than out own fresh fruit and vegetables, and they should have an early claim on any government expenditure and in the framing of government policy with respect to advertising. Growers' associations in many parts of the United States have for many years been conducting intensive advertising campaigns for the marketing of citrus fruits in Canada, and I think their efforts should be met without any further delay by a campaign on behalf of our own growers.
As the member for Essex South (Mr. Clark) said, one who has not made a detailed and comprehensive study of the fruit and vegetable industry in Canada is apt to consider it as somewhat of an orphan industry, but actually it is one of our great agricultural industries and is growing rapidly. I trust the minister will consider taking advantage of this opportunity to assist so far as may be possible by dominion grants in the promotion of a great scheme of advertising and marketing of our fresh fruits and fresh vegetables. I make that suggestion to the minister knowing his sympathetic interest, as expressed the other night, with the growers in different parts of Canada, and I should like to have a statement from him as to what he thinks might be done along these lines.
I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to defer my statement until we get to item 12, which has to do with marketing.

I agree with what the hon. member for Peel has just said. I believe in an advertising campaign-
[Mr. GraydottJ
Might I then suggest, if my hon. friend agrees with him, that we leave the discussion of that until we reach item 12, which has to do with marketing and advertising?

I do not necessarily
agree that advertising alone will solve the problem I have in mind, but rather subsidies by the government of the shipment of fruit from British Columbia.

That has all to do
with marketing, Mr. Chairman, and I would ask the hon. member to discusss it on the other item.

In the second report on
marketing which we received the other day, there is a paragraph on page 10, paragraph 4, which reads as follows:
The seed of a particularly promising new variety of tomato has been purchased. It has been distributed among canners throughout Canada who have undertaken to have the crop produced and processed under the supervision of the Department of Agriculture.
I would ask the minister what companies have been asked to cooperate in this scheme, and in what parts of the country the demonstration is taking place.

We purchased a small
amount of this seed for investigational purposes, which encouraged others to purchase larger amounts, and there has been a general distribution through the two activities. Much of the work is being carried on by the canners themselves.

What companies have the
seed which has been purchased by the department, and in what part of the country have these experiments been carried on?

The department has
the seed which has been purchased by the government, and is experimenting with it. The companies are purchasing seed and having it distributed among their customers.

Is this experimentation
being done by the department at the experimental farms?
Yes.
It says here that the canners are carrying on under supervision of the department.
The canners are carrying it on jointly, with the seed they purchased, as the result of this experiment which has been arranged by the department.

Could the minister give us
any idea in what part of the country this experiment has been carried on?
Supply-Agriculture-M arke ling
It is altogether in Ontario. As a matter of fact it is starting this year.

I am particularly interested in this item. The minister said a few minutes ago that more canned vegetables and fruits were grown and processed in three provinces, two in the eastern part of the country and one in the west. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are more vegetables processed than in any other part of the country. Last year the territory from Napanee, Ontario, on the east, to Peterborough on the west, produced approximately fifty per cent of all the vegetables canned in Canada. Not only that, but approximately fifty per cent of all the exports to foreign countries took place from that territory. There is an abundance of tomatoes grown and processed in those two counties which I represent, and I was deeply interested when I read this item that seed had been purchased. I thought that the department may have looked up the county of Prince Edward, which produces more tomatoes than any other county in Canada and has an ideal soil for their production. If this experiment is to be continued there certainly should be a demonstration lot in that county in order that the canners in that part of the country may benefit by the production of this kind of tomato.

I should like to second what the hon. member (Mr. Tustin) has been saying with regard to the new variety of tomato which is being introduced into Canada. The canners themselves, I believe, are alive to the situation. They have been making a study of what is required in the British market, and I believe that it is the small tomato which is most popular there; when it goes into the can it does not break up as our present-day product does. I have an idea that the canners themselves, rather than the Department of Agriculture, are largely responsible for what is being undertak-m. However, that is aside from what I wanted to mention to the minister at this time.
The packaging and grading of fruit and vegetables are a very important part of the work of this department. Not only should these products be properly packaged and graded but they should be consistent in quality. Too often we hear that different packs of fruit and vegetables from different orchards and localities, though both graded number one, are not alike in grade and in quality. In my opinion, contrary to what has been said by some hon. members this afternoon, not only have we not too many inspectors 51952-1875
but perhaps we have not enough. In regard to the grading of tomatoes, which I understand has been undertaken to a certain extent at the canning factories: when the price spreads commission was investigating certain matters, one of the complaints that were made was that the farmers were not always satisfied with the grade which was given them when they brought their tomatoes in wagon lots and truck loads to the canning factory. I think that arrangements have been made to have government graders at different times and in different places at these factories to see that the grade is properly given, but it would be a good thing if we could have at each of the canning factories where tomatoes are coming in in large lots, just during the canning season, government graders all the time to see that the farmers get the grade to which they are entitled, that they have not to accept the grade which comes from the canning factory owners themselves. Even if it is the fair grade some people may be inclined to think they are not getting a square deal. To make sure that they do, is, I think, in the interest not only of the farmer but also of the canner. I should like to know what the department is doing in this respect. I understand that action is being taken. How far has the work proceeded?

In so far as the matter of grades is concerned, and some showing a little better classification under the grads than others, all that a government grade can do is set a minimum that each one must reach who gets into that grade; there is no way in which a government can or would desire to prevent someone from classifying above that grade. That is, some persons who are desirous perhaps of reaching a certain market may put a better grade of commodity into a certain pack, and call it No. 1, than another person may put into his, but still the lower pack may be above the minimum of the grade. Of course that depends a good deal on the market which the individual is trying to serve, or, perhaps, the way in which he thinks he can best benefit himself by making the pack.
In connection with the matter of full time inspection in certain plants, the government has been and is prepared to supply government inspectors to plants for full time service, provided the plants are prepared to pay the costs. A certain number of plants are willing to do that. They do not pay the inspectors; they remunerate the government for the cost. The inspector is a government official, paid by the government and not by a company. That has been done and can be done under the system now in operation. But the government has not found it possible-largely be-
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

cause of some of the criticism we have heard, even in the house during these estimates, to the effect that we have too many inspectors on the road now,-to meet the wishes of both groups, those who think we should have enough for full time inspection in all factories, and those who think that we have too many of them going the rounds. We try to compromise by saying that where persons are prepared to meet the expense we are prepared to give the service for full time, otherwise they take the same service as anyone else gets.

I am glad to know the department has gone as far as the minister says in furnishing inspectors when they are paid for by the canning factories themselves, but that does not answer the criticism of the farmer. The farmer is the man who thinks he is not being justly treated, and I believe that in justice to the farmer himself something should be done even to make it compulsory that canning factories in their operations, as a condition of getting their licences, should employ government inspectors full time. Not only are they thereby protecting the farmers' interests but they are safeguarding themselves from criticism. I do not believe anybody will criticize a government inspector who is there doing the best work that he can. Frankly speaking, I do not think we have too many inspectors engaged in the grading and inspection of our packaged products. If we are to continue to enter the foreign markets we must put up the best product we can, and that product must be uniform in grade and quality. In spite of what the minister has said about certain shippers who put up products which are above the grade, it seems to me that we should have, particularly for grade 1, the very highest possible quality if we are to compete successfully in the markets of the world, particularly in Great Britain. The minister would be well advised before another fall comes around to make provision that in all these large canning factories and institutions under licence, one of the conditions of getting the licence should be to have a government inspector to look after the grading of the farmers' products.

There is a feeling among the growers-perhaps in some instances there is not a great deal of justification for it-that there is a lack of cooperation between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of National Revenue as regards the time at which the dumping duties are placed upon various imported fruits and vegetables, particularly vegetables. I think it is only right to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. I do not wish to be unduly critical 
because I can quite appreciate the difficulties that face both departments. It is my desire to be extremely fair in this connection. As someone has very aptly said, however, with respect to the importation of vegetables, time [DOT] is of the essence of the whole matter, and a few days' difference in the application of the dumping regulations may mean either success or failure to the Canadian grower. In the main, perhaps, not a great deal of criticism can be offered, but this year certain complaints did reach me as representative of one of the great vegetable-growing sections of central Ontario that the dumping duty on asparagus was perhaps a little late going on. I want to pass that complaint on to the minister, because from now on I think there should be a more careful survey of the production end of the industry and a note made of the exact time when the crop is ready for marketing here.
I repeat. I do not wish to be particularly critical of these two departments, but I want to voice the feeling that I have heard on many occasions and to point out to the minister how very essential it is that the dumping duties be applied at the right time and not seven or eight days too late, as some have suggested that, in certain instances in the past, they have been. I should like the minister to assure the committee that steps will be taken to see that no recurrence of this sort of criticism will be possible in the future.

Before the minister replies to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) I would ask him to look carefully over the applications made during the past three years and compare them with those of the previous five years. If he does so he will find that there has been wonderful cooperation between the two departments mentioned in order to achieve the results that we have seen in the past three years.

I did not expect my remarks to bring the hon. member to his feet quite so quickly, though I know what a great interest he takes in the growers there. I hasten to assure the minister that I was not attempting to compare the work of different governments; in fact, I am not interested in any such comparison, no matter how good either of them may have been in their time. I am simply trying as a humble representative of a vegetable growing section to see that the minister takes proper steps to safeguard the interests of the growers in the future. What I am interested in is the future, not the past.

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

The question under discussion is really one for the Department of National Revenue. The dumping duties are put on through that department and the dates are finally determined by them. They simply seek information from our inspectors who are about the country and act upon it as they see fit. I may tell the hon. gentleman that there is the closest cooperation between the two departments.

My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Graydon) does not entirely approve of the number of cars of vegetables bought in the Holland marsh district. There was a very large production of vegetables in that district, and I believe that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) will substantiate that statement. The people there were having difficulty in getting rid of their vegetables at a price that would give them any profit after paying their costs of production. I entirely disagree with the hon. member for Peel on this point and I want to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture not only on the scheme he put into effect but on the way it was carried out and on the cooperation the growers in that district received from the officials of his department. I also congratulate the department upon having purchased direct from the growers instead of dealing through any middlemen, thus ensuring to the producer the full results of his labour. On behalf of the vegetable growers of Holland Landing I want to express our appreciation of the kindness and efficiency of the department in connection with this service.

The hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock) said he was glad these vegetables were bought from the individual growers of Holland Landing. I am not opposing the purchase of these vegetables, because if they had not been purchased by the government the growers would have received nothing at all for their stuff; it was simply rotting away, and it was a godsend for Holland Landing and my good friend from York North that this did happen. But I notice that the Toronto papers gave credit
Suppl y-Agric ulture-M a the tin g

to the hon. member and to the member of the local legislature for having influenced the minister in order to get him to come there and buy the stuff in Holland Landing. And I should like to ask the minister if he did pay the individual farmers for their stuff, or if he did not appoint an agent to buy the stuff for him. What is the use of making statements like that? No government would go around the country paying individual farmers for the stuff they put in the ears; it is always done through an agent.
I am not going to condemn this government for the wrong things they have done any more than I would condemn any other government, but in the past the governments have not put on the seasonal tariff soon enough or have taken it off too soon. The hon. member for Peel has said that previously the government removed the embargo or seasonal tariff on asparagus too soon or did not take it off soon enough; our own stuff was coming on the market and the influx of American vegetables was ruining the price. That has happened every year, no matter what government has been in power. You go to the Department of Agriculture and they say the Department of National Revenue puts on or takes off the tariff or embargo. You go to the Department of National Revenue and they say, "We do not do it; we do as we are told by the Department of Agriculture." Then you go back to the Department of Agriculture and they say, "We take our information from the horticultural council," and there is no responsibility anywhere. That is the whole trouble; there is no one who knows his job, either in this department, in the horticultural council or in the Department of National Revenue; there is no one to say when the seasonal tariff should be either put on or taken off. and they never listen to anyone who does know anything about it.
The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) mentioned the fact that we had 137 fruit and vegetable inspectors. Then the Minister of Agriculture comes along and says there are 42 inspectors in Prince Edward Island, 88 in Nova Scotia, 43 in New Brunswick, 92 in British Columbia and 77 in Ontario. Can anyone tell me what justification there is for having 42 inspectors in Prince Edward Island?
Just part time

They are just chasing each other around the island, that is all, doing nothing at all. I am just as fond of Prince Edward Island as anyone else, and the growers there are to be congratulated because they need practically no inspectors at all. Their packing and grading are so perfect that they have

made markets for themselves in all parts of the world, and as long as they continue to pack and grade in this way they will never lose those markets. I think 14 inspectors would be sufficient for the whole island. Then you have 43 inspectors in New Brunswick. What do they inspect? You have 88 inspectors in Nova Scotia. What is there but a few apples down in the Annapolis valley? I will say they need some inspectors to watch them, because as yet they have not learned to pack an honest package. They need a little education there in regard to packing. Some hon. members may differ with me, but I know what I am talking about. I have shipped their products to the old country, and the result was not as good as it might have been; it was not very satisfactory. Nova Scotia has 88 inspectors. Can anyone say that SS inspectors are justified there? What can they be doing?
In British Columbia there are 92 inspectors, and there fhey grow a great many commodities that are not produced in the other provinces. But they have learned a little more honesty in the last few years than was formerly the case. I can remember when it was difficult to get anything honest from British Columbia, but to-day their apples, tomatoes and many other products are coming in honestly packed, and reflecting credit upon the country. Today their apples are taking the place of apples from Oregon and Washington in the United States because of their honest packing, but they were forced to do it; they could not get a market until they did. You cannot make farmers honest; if they do not want to be honest the inspectors cannot force them to be, and no one can find a market except by shipping an honest package, it does not matter how many inspectors you have on the job. Then you have only 77 inspectors for Ontario, a province which I think grows more fruit and vegetables than any other province in Canada.

They do not need to be
watched.

No; the packing situation in Ontario is not very good either. We have had a great deal of nonsense in Ontario, but I must say that the packing of the fruit growers in Ontario has improved wonderfully in recent years. They are putting up splendid, honest packages of peaches and other commodities in the Niagara district, which are satisfying the public, but they did not do that until they were forced to it.

How about apples?

They are not so well graded in Ontario as in British Columbia; they are more on a par with Nova Scotia. I could mention individuals who have large orchards in Ontario who are grading splendidly, but I am sorry to say that does not apply to the whole province. They do not believe in grading; for instance, you cannot get Ontario to grade potatoes at all. Some two or three years ago the county of Simcoe tried to force the potato growers to grade their potatoes and stamp them showing that they came from that county, but the attempt was not very successful. My hon. friend from Peel thinks his county is the best in the country; it is a very good county, and I know it very well. They grow a large quantity of good stuff, but they also grow some bad stuff. They have some honest packers and some who are not so good. The situation in regard to the grading of potatoes in Ontario is a crime. If in Ontario potatoes were graded as they are in Prince Edward Island, properly inspected and properly graded; if the best commercial grades were planted, as in Prince Edward Island, Irish cobblers and green mountains, they would keep Prince Edward Island potatoes out of Ontario entirely. In place of that last winter I saw Prince Edward Island potatoes selling for $1 and $1.10 a bag, while Ontario potatoes were selling for 50 cents. The bad condition has been drawn to the attention of the potato growers again and again, but they shovel everything into the bags-potatoes broken at the ends; potatoes broken by the implements used to dig them up; small ones and large ones, hollow ones and everything else. What we need is a little education along this line in Ontario, and I hope we will get it Then you start the marketing board, at great cost to the country. I hate to talk about that, because it was the biggest mess ever started in this country. How could a bunch of young fellows, without any experience whatever, knowing nothing about ports throughout the country, not knowing where to find a market for anything, come into the department and expect to market successfully our product as against men who have had twenty-five, thirty-five and forty years of experience? Yet the advice the minister gets is all from young, innocent kids around the department who know nothing about it. Then you bring a professor from the college at Kingston-no, I did not say the penitentiary -and make him deputy minister. He may be the most able man in the world; he must be very highly educated and all that, but still he lacks the experience he needs for the marketing of anything, no matter what it is. It is a pity the government interferes so
much in business. That is what is ruining the United States to-day. That is what is ruining this country, and what is making conditions so bad. We are interfering too much with business people. To-day there is no encouragement for a man with means at his disposal to put it into anything because he is afraid of the government stealing it from him. We could restore this country to a normal condition much faster if we kept our hands out of other people's business, and gave some encouragement to the man who has money to invest. He feels now that if he makes an investment we will steal it from him.
But I am getting away from the subject of fruit and vegetables. When I say there are too many inspectors of all kinds I could go on to a discussion of entomology, and refer to a bunch of fellows who are going around the country picking up bugs here and there off nursery stock received from foreign countries, and particularly from Holland. The shippers in Holland are as particular to-day as are the people in Canada-I believe they are even more particular. Their only market is their export market. They have to be very sure that the stuff is properly inspected, and it is carefully watched before it comes here. Yet we have an army of inspectors who go all over Canada making inspection. They will pick up an evergreen and stand for half an hour turning a leaf back and forth looking for a bug, but they would not find one in fifty years. I have been importing stuff from Holland for twenty years, including evergreens, fancy trees and shrubs of all kinds, and yet I have never had trouble with them. The insects are killed by fumigation. In Holland everything that is exported is fumigated. Even the moss which is packed around the roots is fumigated and sterilized. They cannot afford to lose their market, and if they did not pack properly they would lose it.
These inspectors are decent fellows, and one could not say an unkind word to any of them. They always have a kind answer for one. In that respect they are like the secretary of the civil service commission You can write to him a thousand times and you will get a thousand letters back, each letter increasing in length. First you will get half a page, next almost a whole page and then you will get three pages. They are the most complete business letters you ever saw, but if you ever got anything out of them in your life I never did. The Department of Agriculture is the same.
Then, there is other extravagance in the Department of Agriculture. The minister must know more about it than he professes

to know. To my mind he is not stupid; in fact I think he is alert. If he were managing a job for himself he would make more examinations than he is making. He accepts all these increases in salary, increases amounting to $28,000. This country is no more prosperous to-day than it was ten years ago; people are no better off. Perhaps this may not be the proper item on which to discuss the matter which has been under debate, but as we have returned from time to time to a discussion of the shipments of fruits, vegetables and other products to the drought area, it might be well if I were to read the full statement with regard to these purchases of commodities, so that everyone may read it in Hansard. It is as follows:
Owing to suffering throughout a large part of Saskatchewan and a portion of eastern Alberta which became most acute in the year 1937, due to continued crop failures, and also owing to the fact that there were large surpluses of foodstuffs in the eastern provinces wrhich promised to glut the market and thus cause distress among the farmers by lack of an opportunity to sell their products or to sell only at ruinous prices, the dominion government decided to purchase certain food supplies and send to the farmers of the stricken areas of the west.
Supplies were purchased under governor general's warrant, P.C. 2422, chiefly in the maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia. By agreement between the federal government and the government of the province of Saskatchewan certain 177 rural municipalities and local improvement districts in the province of Saskatchewan were designated as the areas which had suffered most from the crop failures of the past eight years and hence were entitled to share in this special distribution of food supplies.
Similarly, by agreement betw'een the federal government and the government of the province of Alberta certain 50 rural municipalities and local improvement districts in Alberta were designated to share in this special distribution. The Dominion Department of Agriculture issued instructions as to the allotment of the supplies on the basis of five to a family. The instruc-

Supply-Agriculture-M arke ting
tions were as follows: 30 pounds of cheese; 33 pounds of beans; 150 pounds of apples; 44 pounds of fish; 100 pounds of turnips and 150 pounds of other vegetables.
These instructions were followed as closely as possible. A total of 285 cars of apples, 142 cars of turnips, 242 cars of cabbage, carrots, parsnips and beets and 220 cars of assorted fish, cheese and beans (these latter 200 cars being reshipped ex Regina after being warehoused and repacked) were shipped to their various destinations by this office.
Population figures for the rural areas and for the incorporated towns and villages were secured through the provincial governments and later checked and verified by the local municipalities. The carloads were broken down to the nearest eighth part to fill the requirements for each municipality or district. The cars of apples and vegetables were spotted direct to their destination. The cars containing fish, cheese and beans were all spotted for Regina where the contents were warehoused, repacked into suitable size for distribution and then reshipped to their ultimate destination. This involved a great deal of warehouse space. At one time as many as sixty-six men were engaged in the task of preparing the fish, cheese and beans for distribution to 73,450 homes.
The weather was favourable, especially during the weeks that the apples and vegetables were being handled. Only two carloads, one a refrigerator car and one a box car, both containing carrots, were partially destroyed by frost. From each of these cars from one-quarter to three-eighths was saved for human consumption, the balance of the two cars being distributed for cattle feed.
Only two cases of demurrage at railway points were reported, both being for one day duration.
Only two complaints were received as to shortage in cars which could be chargeable to the shippers. Particulars of these cases were immediately reported to the Department of Agriculture, Ottawa. Two complaints were also received with regard to the quality of the commodity, one being with respect to two barrels of apples from Nova Scotia and the other that the dried fish was unfit for use. This latter complaint, upon investigation, was found due to the fact that the complainant did not know how to prepare the food for the table. From every municipality and district without exception have come reports of the excellent quality of the supplies furnished.
The recipes sent by the Dominion Department of Agriculture as to the best way of preparing fish, cheese and beans for the table were greatly appreciated and added much to the value of the foodstuffs provided by the government.
The responsibility of distributing the supplies throughout the towns, villages and rural municipalities was placed upon the shoulders of the secretary-treasurers, reeves and councillors and the overseers of the towns. They measured up to a very difficult task and discharged their duties in a fair and efficient manner. No one who had a right to be served was purposely overlooked. It is no small task to divide the contents of 879 carloads of food supplies among 367,250 people over wide and often thinly populated areas to the satisfaction of all. Very few complaints have come in and adjustments were made when found necessary. Special mention should be made of the work of the secretary-treasurers of the rural municipalities. Upon
them fell the work of directing the task of distribution. Immediately upon allotment of cars or parts of cars the municipal secretaries were reached by telephone. This was considered in the best interests of distribution since the prairie winter weather was close at hand, and also in order that information should be relayed throughout the districts concerned to insure the quickest possible delivery to the people. It was decided that mailing of instructions was too uncertain since this entire movement of freight was not going on regular schedule but by special trains which were being routed on all lines at all times. Telephoning also ensured that instructions as to forwarding parts of cars from one municipality to another were properly understood and any points regarding any of the work about which officials were in doubt could be fully explained.
The railroads gave the best of service. Special mention should be made of the fine cooperation given by Mr. W. J. Anderson, district freight agent of the Canadian Pacific Railway and by Mr. R. E. Johnston, district freight agent of the Canadian National Railways. They did everything in their power to assist in the smooth working of the plans for speedy distribution.
The supplies sent out by the federal government have been greatly appreciated by the people who received them. We have a large file of letters which have been sent to us from ratepayers' associations, congregations of churches, community clubs and individuals expressing their appreciation and sincere thanks. Frequently the high quality of the foodstuffs is referred to and also the fairness of distribution made by the municipal councils.
I have the costs of distribution down to the date of this report if they are of interest to hon. members.

The minister has just read to us a very detailed statement, and I think it was proper that that statement should have been given at this time. I am not complaining about the manner in which the distribution took place, apart from the complaints I made yesterday in connection with the distribution having been general. I should like to ask the minister if the department made any effort, to secure any vegetables last year in the northern part of Saskatchewan. They had a bountiful harvest of vegetables in that part of the province and I understand that certain municipalities offered to collect several carloads for distribution in the southern part. I should like to know also if any effort was made to obtain fish from the northern part of the province. It is well known that the lakes in the north are teeming with fish and there was a part of the season when any fish caught could have been kept frozen. While I am on my feet I may as well ask another question I had in mind. The statement just read by the minister referred to certain demurrage having been paid in Regina. The minister also mentioned that Doctor Stapleford had been employed to superintend the distribution. I wonder if it would be possible for him to give the committee the correspondence that took place with Doctor Stapleford in connection with his employment. Earlier in the session we were told that this gentleman was receiving S500 a month and expenses to carry on this work. When the people of Saskatchewan found that out there was considerable criticism. I do not think the public generally knew that this gentleman was receiving that amount for doing this work. For many years Doctor Stapleford had received a salary from Regina college and the church to which he belonged. Later on he was employed by the university. I understand he was then retired on superannuation and had accepted a position as assistant prin-

cipal of a college in Ontario. I should like to know why it was thought necessary to employ Doctor Stapleford to do this work. I have no doubt that there were 500 people in Saskatchewan who would have done this work voluntarily, or at least for a dollar a day and expenses. The minister has stated that the distribution was made in 177 rural municipalities. The mayors of these municipalities gave of their services freely. The clergy in the towns also gave their services free, and in view of all the work that was done voluntarily I think it was an outrage that this man should have been employed to do the work at that salary. The members of the relief commission under the late government gave their services free. It was managed by Mr. Daniel and consisted of four or five business men, one or two from the city of Regina, one from Moose Jaw, and a farm woman, who also gave her services free except for her expenses while in Regina. Then consider that this work under this government was done by a man who was paid $500 a month! I would like to have the correspondence relating to his appointment, and a statement from the minister as to why it was necessary to employ this man, who was drawing a superannuation allowance, and as well I believe an annuity from the university of Saskatchewan.

So far as Doctor Stapleford himself is concerned, many members both in the east and in the west know him personally, and I do not need to make any apologies for him. He is known to leading business men from one end of Canada to the other, and everyone who knows him will acknowledge him to be not only one of the foremost educationalists- one important eastern university has just engaged him for a very important financial task-'but also a man who for directing the business side of an institution is one of the best we have in Canada; and he has been recognized as such in all parts of Canada.
The only reason he was leaving Saskatchewan was that the church college, which had been operated in Regina for many years, and is one of the best educational institutions in the western provinces, was taken over by the university of Saskatchewan and is now being operated under the president of that university. The church did not desire to continue with it longer; when it was taken over by the university Doctor Stapleford found that his duties there were not in exact accordance with his desires, and he later was offered the position he now occupies with Victoria university in Toronto. He was a graduate of that institution and was taken back there to do work in connection with the financial side of their set-up.
' The churches had been doing a great deal of work on a voluntary basis in connection with the distribution of food sent from eastern Canada to western Canada. On a number of occasions I had had discussions with the head of the United church, the superintendent of missions of the United church, and representatives of other churches in regard to the matter. I discussed with them this particular distribution in its relation to their distribution before we undertook it. Throughout the discussions which took place between those who were interested in the distribution of their own products and myself as interested in the distribution to be made by the Department of Agriculture, we were in agreement that there was no better man in Canada to do the job and no man whose appointment would be more acceptable to the people generally than Doctor Stapleford.
It might be suggested that he should have done this work for a lower salary than was paid him, and there might be some justification for that view were it not for the fact that that was the lesser of the two jobs that he had to do. Doctor Stapleford was asked to take over these duties and see to the coordinating of the work of this organization with that of the voluntary organizations, and he was asked at the same time to make a
complete report to the government of Canada upon the giving of relief in western Canada dating back as far as governments have been giving relief. When the late government started their relief activities in 1930 or 1931 I venture to say they were in much the same position as that in which we found ourselves when we took over the government in 1935, that no authentic information on relief distribution was to be had anywhere. Unless you searched the files of municipal, provincial and federal departments of government from one end to the other in order to find out, there was no authentic information available upon which to base any action in connection with the handling of relief in these different areas. An expenditure of $8,700,000 was made in 1914-15 alone, and since Doctor Stapleford has been at the task of compiling in one volume all the information with regard to past distributions of relief I have found that in common with every other public speaker who has been delivering addresses in western Canada I have been making misstatements in regard to the distribution of relief. I looked up all the information I could find upon it in certain departments and I gave that information to the public, but when I had the complete information in my hands I found I have been giving some information that was not correct.
I think every member of this committee will agree, since apparently we are going to have these periods of drought in western Canada, that it is essential that we should have available an authentic report of what has taken place in the distribution of relief from away back in the eighties down to the present, so that the information may be available when one of these difficult periods recurs. Doctor Stapleford has performed that task. He has placed in the hands of the government a complete report in so far as it could be found in the records of departments and of governments either at Ottawa or in western Canada, of all the activities of municipal, provincial and federal governments and relief organizations, voluntary and otherwise, in regard to the handling of the problem particularly of giving direct relief to the people of western Canada.

Would the minister answer the first two questions, with respect to the purchase of vegetables and fish?

In so far as the purchase of vegetables in western Canada is concerned, I believe we purchased about thirty-nine cars, mostly in Manitoba, a few in Alberta, and I am not sure that a few were not purchased in Saskatchewan, but they were very few. The first reason why we bought so few in Saskatchewan is that there were not many vegetables in that province. We had almost the most complete crop failure in Saskatchewan last year that we ever had; and while we speak of the 170 municipalities referred to as the "hundred per cent drought area," it does not by any means cover the whole drought area of the province in that year. The drought area extended right up into the northern section, and though certain municipalities had a surplus of vegetables, it also happened that alongside of them were muni-

cipalities which had to get vegetables. We did not think it fair to go into the northern area where there might be a surplus in a comparatively small district, and compete with some municipality alongside it in purchasing vegetables required by those individuals. In other words the policy was to go into districts where there were surpluses which might be a drug on the market, and purchase them and distribute them in the drought areas.
As far as the fish are concerned, if the desire was only to take fish out of the lakes and freeze them, we probably would not have had to go up into the northern area. My hon. friend knows that the Qu'Appelle lakes, alongside my farm and his own, are full of fish.
And lots of men there.

There are, of course, men there who can and do fish, and who fished last year and sold fish as they had done previously. I venture to say that smoked fish-salted cod and that sort of thing-does not enter into competition veiy actively with fresh fish in areas where fresh fish is easily available, but it nevertheless forms the basis of a diet which is very healthful; and in better times, when these people who last year were eating dried cod and smoked herring for the first time in their lives are looking for some tasty food, they will probably go down to the mari-times to get it. That is one of the reasons we took the action we did.

They made an awful mess of it.

That information was available. True enough, he had been principal of Regina college, and no doubt he made a very good

The first question is:
To what extent has the economic distress of the past few years in the rural area of your constituency affected the morale (1) of individuals, (2) of the community as a whole?
Then it goes on:

I was coming to that. I mentioned that it went to both federal and provincial members. I believe that the morale of citizens who have been forced to accept relief under this set-up has been more seriously affected than was that of those who had to accept relief from 1930 to 1934.

I was going to ask the minister if the salt fish was cod fish. Maritime people have told me that some of the fish sent out to western Canada was not cod, and that that was the reason for some of the difficulties, that it was a lower grade fish which they call pollock. I do not think it was pollock such as we knew in the old land, because we did not salt it, but they call it pollock, and some people from the maritimes have told me that that was a cause of dissatisfaction, and that this fish is not cod.

The list I read last evening answers, I think, the hon. member's question-that we purchased a certain amount of cod at 5j cents and a certain amount of pollock at 3 to 3| cents, and it is acknowledged that pollock.is not as good a fish as cod. In the process of distribution an attempt was made to give some of each to each family, but that could not be carried all the way through; it was not possible to give every family exactly the same type of fish. But where one person was given pollock and another cod, it would probably be found that the person who got the pollock had some canned herring and chicken haddock or something of that kind put in as well.
The only point is that so far as advertising the fish of the maritimes is concerned, I am afraid it was not very well advertised by the pollock.
I think the fact that only two complaints came in is a good indication that whatever was sent was pretty well advertised.
Probably they did not write in, but I was in the west recently, and I heard some interesting stories and more interesting remarks about the salt fish.
Would the minister answer my question with respect to superannuation?
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has asked me about the superannuation which was allowed to Doctor Staple-ford. All I can say is that I do not know anything about it.
That does not answer the second question.

It answers it as far as I am concerned. I do not think it is any of the business of the government whether Doctor Stapleford is getting a superannuation allowance from some other concern or not. We did not hire him because he was getting superannuation or was not getting it. We hired him because we thought he could do the job.

What progress has been made in developing a market in Canada for sweet cider? I understand that at present there are some shipments of sweet eider to England, and I wondered whether any progress had been made in developing a market at home. I have a pleasant recollection of cider, and I should like to see the market extended. Another question: Has there been any development in Canada in connection with a product called powdered apple? I tried to get some information in this connection, but I could not find anything. Perhaps the minister can tell me something about it.

In the latter part of 1937 or early in 1938 great sections of the growers of Ontario and other parts of Canada became alarmed over rumours which were then prevalent with regard to changes that were being made in the protection afforded the vegetable and fruit men in the proposed new agreements to be entered into between the United States

and Canada. The tariff board in 1933 made certain recommendations in answer to an application from the fruit and vegetable growers of Canada. The findings were, in part, that the applicants had made out a case in favour of preserving for the Canadian producer during his growing season a market in the section of the country which he is able to supply. Since the last changes in the agreement between the United States and Canada, which went into effect on January 1, 1936-I am only speaking from memory in this connection, but I think I am right-the increase in general imports from the United States was 33} per cent, whereas the increase in imported vegetables was something like 53 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must call the hon. member to order. The committee is not now discussing the tariff, and I would ask him to confine his remarks to the item under consideration.

This item has to do with fruit and vegetables, and I thought I might be given a little latitude in order to bring out this point. The fruit and vegetable growers believe that they have already assumed more than their fair share of the burden imposed by the trade agreements, and when the new agreements are finally brought before the government for consideration I trust that the Minister of Agriculture will be very careful to protect the interests of the vegetable growers so that there will be no relaxation in the tariff and no easing up so far as the dumping duties are concerned.

There is some question as to procedure in connection with the dumping duties. Who puts on the dumping duties? This is a very important matter, because a good deal depends on the early market. The first goods put on the market always get a good price, and if the dumping duties are not put on at the right time the growers will not get the benefit of that price. The minister might tell us what the procedure is.

The question is one that could be better discussed under the estimates of the Department of National Revenue. They have much more information than we have. They seek information wherever they can get it. They have their own men out getting information and we have our inspectors, who naturally make reports. The Department of National Revenue before making any decision consults the fruit and vegetable branch of the Department of Agriculture, but that is the department that takes action in pursuance of the information it receives from different sources.
