Where does the horticultural society come in?
Officially they do not " come in." They may be consulted like anyone else who is associated with the business. The departments will consult anyone. I have consulted individuals on occasion myself.

lit has been said that this $5,000 paid to the horticultural society is handed over to their secretary and he makes reports as to when these duties should be put on. Is there any truth in that statement?

There is no relation between this $5,000 and any reports that may come from the horticultural society. This arrangement has existed for many years; first it was $8,000, later $4,500 and then, because of the return of the ten per cent, it became $5,000. That goes to the horticultural society, which has a secretary. As I understand it, the same gentleman happens to be secretary for the wholesalers of fruit, and naturally they make representations through their secretary to the Department of National Revenue. They may on occasion even write letters to the Department of Agriculture. Like any other organization that is interested in these things they make representations to the different departments concerned, but the departments make their own decisions as to whether or not they will agree with the recommendations.

In other words this
gentleman gets $5,000 from this government, indirectly, and probably another $5,000 from the other people; he plays both ends against the middle, makes whatever recommendations he wishes, and the government carries them out.
The hon. gentleman is hardly correct in saying that the government makes a grant of $5,000 to the secretary.
I did not say that.
That is about what it amounts to.
Let us put it this way: The government pays the horticultural society $5,000 and the society pays him $5,000. Is that plain enough?

I have no knowledge of what the horticultural society pays him or what the wholesalers pay him. I only know that the same gentleman happens to be secretary of both organizations, because as such he communicates with us from time to time. I presume the organization is quite capable of engaging its own secretary and knowing whether or not he is giving service for the money.

I should like to ask the minister a question about containers:	A short
time ago I was speaking about tomatoes and their grading. The report of the minister for 1937 states that progress is being made towards the standardization of containers for canned fruit and vegetables. That was a very live question when the price spreads commission was investigating certain matters. There appeared to be containers that looked very much alike but which contained entirely different amounts. Could the minister tell us just what progress has been made towards standardization of those containers. It is undoubtedly true that standardization could not be carried out fully in connection with export trade because of the difference in the demands of importing countries in regard to canned goods; containers of the same size would not be suitable for the markets of all countries. But I think it is very important that we should know something of what is being done towards the standardization of containers.

There has been a great deal of activity in the direction of trying to obtain standard containers for the different types of packs, but that is a matter which concerns international trade to such an extent that we must give some thought to what they are doing elsewhere. There is a bill before the United States congress at present having to do with that matter, and the department here is keeping close check on it with the idea that when we finally do something in this regard it will conform fairly closely to what is being done elsewhere.

I should like to ask one more question having to do with the inspection of apples. The Shaw report, so called, among other things has this to say with regard to our shipments of apples to the United Kingdom :
Complaints regarding the variation in the grading of Canadian apples were without doubt in many cases well founded.
And again:
Greater care should be taken to assure that the top layer of apples in a barrel is a fair sample of the whole contents.
Evidently that has not been so in the past. Then in his recommendations he states:
More rigid enforcement of the grading regulations would undoubtedly tend to remove these complaints.
I could mention some other features of the report. As I understand it, the grading and inspection of apples is done at the port, and they are graded only by sample; in fact I understand that only about one sample out
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

of twenty is inspected. It seems to me that more careful inspection of our exports of apples should be maintained, and I would ask the minister just what is contemplated in that direction.

Ordinarily, of course, the inspection consists of about one in twenty, or about five per cent; but as a matter of fact where there is any doubt about it at all the percentage might be much larger than that; perhaps the greater part might be inspected. That is the practice followed. There will be improvement in that connection as we go along, just as was indicated a few moments ago by the hon. member for Parkdale, who I think agreed in part at least with the gentlemen who wrote the report that there were some grounds for complaint in connection with the packs from certain parts of Canada. That complaint is being looked into, and instructions have been given our men to make more careful checks. It is part also of our activities overseas, as the result of the appointment of a man to represent the department there, to have these packs checked more closely on the other side in order to try to maintain our standard at as high a level as possible.

This report also states that American and Canadian apples are sent to the old country at about the same season of the year; that Canadian apples are frequently looked upon by the trade as American, and are sometimes sold as such. Has the department any idea that Canadian apples or the packages containing them might be marked differently so that they could be recognized in the market over there as being Canadian apples, or could any method be devised by which this might be brought about?

There has been no decision with regard to apples, as to whether or not we will apply the standard mark to them; but that is the whole basis of the standard mark, to have it put on the high standard products in order that they may be identified as Canadian.

But that applies only to the container, and once a barrel of apples is opened up the person who buys them in the retail store does not see the container and is not in a position to know whether or not they are Canadian apples. I understand that most of the apples shipped in hampers are wrapped in tissue paper or cellophane or something of the kind; these wrappings at least might bear the word "Canada" so that our apples may be known as such.

There is no difficulty about the apples that are wrapped with paper and shipped in boxes; those can be marked just as Sunkist oranges are marked. But with apples packed in barrels, as they are in Nova Scotia, there might be greater difficulty in having that mark appear. One can see from that what might be a standard mark in one place would be difficult to apply in the same way in another place.

Item agreed to.
Live stock and poultry, $537,339.

I notice an increase of approximately $55,000 in this item, which is indicative of the importance of this branch of agriculture. Live stock should be regarded as one of the main factors in successful agriculture. Anyone who has had the experience will substantiate that statement. The breeding, feeding and marketing of live stock is therefore very important.
It seems to me that our domestic market must be given some careful consideration. I have read in the Ottawa papers where dressed beef can be purchased for ten cents a pound. That beef is sold in the market in Ottawa. Then, we notice advertisements in the paper showing that better cuts of meat sell for thirty-five cents per pound. But when one goes to a restaurant he pays $1.50 per pound. In order to assure myself that I was not exaggerating I went to one of the leading butcher shops in Ottawa and asked how much beefsteak a restaurant would serve on an order. The reply was that ordinarily they would serve eight ounces and, in rare cases, ten ounces. When we consult a bill of fare we find we are charged seventy-five cents or eighty cents and sometimes a dollar for a beefsteak, but we are receiving only half a pound. It is for that reason I say that we are being charged at the rate of $1.50 per pound. This matter received consideration by the legislature of Manitoba in the present year when it appointed a special committee to investigate the matter. It might be in order to go farther and ask the dominion parliament to undertake an investigation along similar lines.
What else, for which there is no stated charge, does the hon. member get with the beefsteak?

You get a lot of frills which do not appease your appetite. I would be satisfied with the service I would get with a beefsteak costing fifty cents, because I think that should be the outside price for one.
When I rose to speak I had in mind chiefly the marketing of fresh beef in the old country.

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
Some time ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture if any investigation had taken place in connection with the placing of fresh killed beef on the British market. I received the answer that in 1921 the Harris Abattoir, which is now connected with Canada Packers, made a trial shipment. I was told, further, that in 1923 the dominion government had made a trial shipment, and that in 1934 the university of Saskatchewan had made one. I have no knowledge as to the outcome of the shipments made by the university of Saskatchewan and the dominion government, but I have a distinct recollection of the matter being discussed in the house in 1922 and 1923 after the trial shipment was made by the Harris Abattoir. The shipment proved that our meat met with satisfaction in the old country market, and it sold on a par with British killed meat, and at a substantial premium over chilled and frozen meat from the Argentine. I wonder why this market has not been developed, and why our great packing institutions have not developed the placing of fresh killed beef on the British market. I do not know the reason, but sometimes I think the fact that the packing industry in Great Britain and on this continent are vitally interested financially in the meat business of the Argentine, and that might be the reason why they have not undertaken to develop the fresh meat trade with the old country. As the trade would be developed, it would displace exports from the Argentine. It seems to me that some government agency must undertake this work if we are going to make any advance.
When we read the report submitted by the committee which was sent overseas we find the project is altogether feasible, and that there is a distinct advantage in undertaking this work. At this point I should like to read to the committee an article written by Miss Cora Hind, agricultural editor of the Winnipeg Free Press. I read the article because Miss Hind is, I believe, one of the greatest authorities on the continent in agricultural matters. It will be remembered that about two years ago she made a tour of different countries in the world, following which tour she submitted a report of her travels, and made particular mention of the possibility of placing fresh killed beef on the British market. The article is headed "British Market is Open for Meat" and is in these words:
In regard to live stock and the products thereof, I am firmly convinced, after my three months in the Argentine, that Canada, and for that matter Australia and New Zealand, can never successfully and profitably compete with the Argentine in the matter of chilled meat
for the British market. In time, and at very considerable expense for sires, Canada could undoubtedly produce the quality but not at the price. Some of the Canadians who scoff at the idea of Canada putting fresh killed, grain finished beef on the London market may be surprised to know how men on the Argentine frigorificos are alive to that possibility and that more than once I was asked as to the likelihood of Canada doing it.
It might be well for Canada to get busy on this scheme before a generation in England has grown so used to the tender but really rather tasteless Argentinian chilled beef that it will refuse to pay higher prices for Canadian grain finished, fresh killed beef. Doors that may have stood open and inviting for a long time, when never used, have an uncanny habit of closing in the face of those who, long neglecting, suddenly decide to use them.
The question of fresh killed beef on the British market has long since passed the experimental stage, and I am glad indeed the minister has decided to undertake the work. Perhaps it will be done only on a limited scale at the present time. However, if he will develop the market I have no doubt in the world that we have the facilities and the farmers who desire and are able to furnish the finest beef grown in the world. I refer, of course, to grain-fed baby beef.
A few moments ago I said the packing institutions of Canada have had about seventeen years experience in connection with the project, but have not developed the trade. It seems to me the government should step in. My suggestion would be that it should lend assistance to some cooperative society which would place the meat on the British market. The government might build an abattoir, or lend to some other organization at a low rate of interest the money necessary for that purpose. At some point on the Atlantic coast there should be a year-round port from which Canadian beef could be shipped to the British market. Our beef could be placed on refrigerator ships and be delivered in the British butcher shops ready for cutting up. It would have to be hung for a period of ten or twelve days after killing. My belief is that under such arrangements it would arrive in the British market in the pink of condition.
I have mentioned a cooperative society because the other day, when speaking about Danish bacon, the minister said that this product was bred, fed and sold cooperatively. Every hon. member knows that the selling of Danish bacon in the old country market has been most successful. I believe it fetches a premium over any other bacon on that market.
I am deeply interested in the subject, having been engaged in the live stock industry

all my life. It was a pity the Canadian government got rid of its merchant marine. The government owned marine service would have taken care of the shipments and would have seemed almost like a gift from Santa Claus. However, those ships have been scrapped, but they might have been used in conjunction with our Canadian National railways to carry our beef to market. Despite this handicap, we should go forward in the development of the fresh beef market. I have said more than I intended to say, but I am really interested in this work and I should like the minister to tell the committee what steps have been taken or what advance has been achieved in connection with supplying fresh killed beef to the British market.

The hon. member has just referred to the activities in connection with supplying fresh killed beef to the British market. He stated that he was familiar with the experiment carried on by the Harris Abattoir some years ago. I happen to be familiar with the experiment carried on by the university of Saskatchewan a comparatively few years ago. On that occasion the present director of marketing in the Department of Agriculture was in charge of the agricultural college at the university in Saskatoon. He was really responsible for the experiment that was carried on. That experiment consisted of choosing seventy-five steers. I believe those steers were first on the Matador ranch in Saskatchewan and then they were finished with grain. Twenty-five were killed in Saskatoon and shipped directly to the old country to be sold on the Smithfield market. Twenty-five were shipped to Montreal, killed in an abattoir there and the meat shipped in cold storage to the Smithfield market. The other twenty-five were shipped on foot to Birkenhead, where they were slaughtered and the meat sent to the Smithfield market.
There are certain difficulties to be overcome in undertaking an experiment of this kind. The Canadian railways have no refrigerator cars capable of carrying beef in sides, as it is desired in the old country. Therefore, the meat had to be hung in a way in which it should not be hung in shipping it from Saskatoon to Montreal. The refrigerator cars available in this country have been constructed for the purpose of carrying any commodity that requires cold storage, and it was found that the beef was not heated evenly at the top and bottom of the car. When the meat reached Montreal it had to be handled under the conditions I described the other day in connection with bacon. It had to be taken from the refrigerator cars and moved
FMr. Leader.]
across the wharf, sometimes in great heat, then put into the hold of the boat and taken across the Atlantic. It just happened that when this meat reached the other side the conditions on the Smithfield market were not right for the marketing of it at the end of the week, and it was thought advisable to hold the beef over until Monday, if I remember rightly. That necessitated opening up the hold to take out all the other commodities and then closing it up again and putting the Canadian beef back into storage for another two days. The result was that the beef which had been killed in Saskatoon had undergone about as trying a trip as beef could be expected to undergo. That which was shipped from Montreal encountered conditions a little less difficult. The beef shipped on foot and killed at Birkenhead demonstrated that this was the most efficient manner of placing this product upon that market under the conditions prevailing and with the facilities existing between Saskatoon and London.
My memory of what happened is that the Canadian beef slaughtered at Birkenhead sold at prices which compared very favourably with the best Scottish beef. The beef which was killed in Montreal sold at a little lower price, and that which was killed in Saskatoon sold at a still lower price. My memory is that the beef killed in Montreal sold to better advantage than Argentine chilled beef and demonstrated that beef shipped under those conditions, or under the slightly improved conditions possible to-day, can be sold to advantage as against Argentine beef.

Was the beef that was
slaughtered in Montreal sold at a price sufficiently higher to pay the freight from the west, and was the beef slaughtered in England sold at a price sufficiently higher to pay the ocean freight, which I understand is $15?

The beef shipped on foot and slaughtered in England returned the best price to the individual on this side. The beef slaughtered in Montreal brought the next best return to the individual on this side. The beef killed in Saskatoon brought the lowest return to the individual on this side. With the facilities available it would appear that it would be better to ship the beef on foot. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) is advocating that a change should be made in the conditions; -but, as was indicated the other day, we are carrying on experiments in the hope of providing better facilities, either at Montreal or at some other point, for the transference of beef killed in Canada to ships. All I can say is that the

Suppl y-Agriculture-M arke ting
Argentine trade in beef has been developed over a long term of years. The first thing they did was to provide for careful breeding, and that country has some of the best beef stock to be found anywhere in the world. Another point in t-heir favour is the fact that most of their stock is comparatively near to the seaboard. My understanding is that it is all slaughtered on the wharves and that there is no change in temperature from the time of cooling following killing to the placing on the ships. They have also developed ships which are used only for the carrying of beef, and in which the temperature is constant.
We could ship beef from this country to England to be sold as fresh killed beef. I understand that on the British market beef is considered as fresh killed if it has been slaughtered within ten days. My understanding is that it takes a month to deliver Argentine beef to the British market, and therefore it is shipped in chilled form. We can ship ours as fresh killed beef and sell it in competition with other fresh beef on the British market. However, to do this, facilities must be provided on our wharves and boats must be specially constructed to handle this fresh meat. We would have to use all the space provided in the boat for this purpose.
Is any being shipped now?
We are arranging to ship limited amounts.
How much?

I have not the exact amount. We have entered into an arrangement with the packers to carry out this experiment for us and to undertake shipments to the old country markets for a period of twelve months.
Where will that beef be killed?
Mostly in Toronto.

In carrying out this experiment is consideration being given to the pluck and offal? These are important items in considering the return from an animal. There is a return from the heart and liver and things like that, and the other offal which may be used for fertilizer and other purposes.
Every part of the animal will be accounted for. The liver and offal will not be shipped to the old country. It will be used on this side.
It will be in the returns?

Yes.
Mr. LEADER. My idea is that these cattle should be killed, not in Toronto, but at the Atlantic seaboard. We can raise all
kinds of first-class feeder cattle in western Canada, and are glad to sell them at the market price, and I am sure that the mari-timers would gladly buy them at the market price. If these feeder cattle were slaughtered at the seaboard, the maritimers could fatten them down there, and the fresh killed beef would arrive in the old country at the very lowest possible cost of production. But if they are killed in Toronto, you have to have refrigerator cars to ship them to the seaboard, and transportation costs are greater. We have fooled with this thing long enough. If you are going to make an honest-to-goodness attempt to put fresh killed beef on the British market, then take the best method you can find, something like that used in the Argentine, slaughter the cattle at the seaboard and place it on the market in the shortest possible time. If we adopt the best possible methods, we might be able to win our way with fresh killed beef into the British market.
Why was Toronto selected?

The facilities at the seaboard are not as desired by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, and again Toronto is the one market where you have the greatest number from which to make your selection of high grade beef. That is the condition at present. All factors that enter into cost can be determined. The cost of shipping from Montreal or Toronto, the difference between the cost of shipping live cattle and the dead animal-all these differences will figure in the cost and can be determined.
It is in the nature of an experiment?

Yes, and I do not think it would be advisable for the government or anyone else to enter into the enormous expense involved in building an abattoir at, say Saint John, and putting in the equipment necessary to handle the beef like they do in the Argentine, with a complete line of boats, or even only one boat, to carry on an experiment of this kind. All we can do is to say that we are carrying on the experiment under the most difficult conditions one can possibly prescribe, and if we can succeed under those conditions we could succeed much better if we had better facilities. These facilities might then be provided by private capital. That is the way in which it is done in the Argentine. It is not done by the government there, but three companies do the business
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

largely, one 'being Swifts and another an English organization. They handle the beef direct from the Argentine to Great Britain.
As to what will develop out of the experiment, that will depend upon what has been accomplished when it has been completed and upon the attitude of private interests as to whether they want to go into a business of that kind.

Will there always be sufficient cargo space to take these carcases across? There has been great difficulty in getting boat space for the shipment of live cattle. The difficulty might be overcome if we had the assurance that there would always be sufficient refrigerator space in the vessels to take the fresh killed beef across.

So far as this experiment is concerned, special arrangements are being made covering the whole twelve months, so there will be no difficulty in obtaining space, because the space will be booked and the beef will be put into cold storage weekly throughout the year.

Seeing
that the government is paying for the experiment, would it not have been advisable to do as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has suggested, have the cattle slaughtered at the seaboard and the fresh killed beef shipped from the nearest possible point to the British market? I realize that the experiment may not be profitable in its initial stage, but certainly it would be profitable for this dominion it we could establish a market in the old country for our fresh killed beef. Many people have recognized that for many years, and I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that the shortest possible route to the British market is the one which should have been taken, and the cattle slaughtered at the seaboard. I realize the volume of the business that is done in the city of Toronto, but there would be advantages from a national standpoint to ship, if at all possible, directly from Halifax or Saint John, or even Montreal, although shipments from Montreal would take a day or two longer, and that port could not be used the whole year round. I think the government might well consider the advisability of adopting that suggestion, independently of the extra cost of supplying a smaller quantity. I notice by the minister's report which was given to the house the other day, or perhaps I should say the report of the committee-
Call it mine.

After
looking at the spectacular page ten I think it should certainly be called the minister's report. Paragraph 3 on page ten states:
Arrangements have been completed to have a definite quantity of fresh killed beef forwarded weekly to the London market.
Evidently the arrangements have been made and we are now committed to supplying the British market weekly with our fresh killed beef. Toronto is a long way inland, and subject to the handicaps, to which the minister alluded a few moments ago, of its being necessary to change from car to boat during hot weather conditions. All these are difficulties that have been recognized for some years, and I think they are still difficulties in making the test so far inland successful. I do not know whether the facilities at Halifax would be suitable, but I do think that even at some extra expense the department would have been well advised to ship high class beef animals on the hoof to Halifax or Saint John, no matter how few in number, to see if we could not establish for ourselves a market in Britain and meet the demand by a continuous and regular supply of high class beef. Even Montreal would have been much closer than Toronto, and would have avoided the change from car to boat.
I personally commend the effort which the department is making in this regard, and which I think is only in keeping with what might be done in many lines so far as the export of our meat is concerned, but I do think the government would be well justified in spending even more money to carry out the experiment from the closest possible port to secure the British market. It is in keeping with the suggestion I made here the other day with reference to giving assistance in the marketing of live stock products. Some have said that this is unsound; but I have observed in the old land, in the very market in which we are endeavouring to sell our farm products, they have their bacon development board, and indirectly or almost directly they are giving assistance, even what might be called subsidies, to make up the difference between the market price and the fixed price. I think there would be very little criticism throughout the dominion if the government spent a considerably larger sum to develop this trade, which I believe could be developed more efficiently if we chose the shortest possible route and shipped the beef from the nearest possible point to the British market.

I realize the difficulties on account of lack of facilities at the seaboard, but I should like the minister to

Supply-Agriculture-M arke ting
explain the advantages in shipping the beef dressed over shipping cattle on the hoof as we do now.

The great difficulty, of course, in maintaining our British market has been to maintain a continuous supply in that market. In shipping the beef on foot as we have been doing, there seems to be a tendency on the part of our people, whether it is the producer or those who are handling cattle, to direct shipments for a time, say to the Chicago market, because temporarily the price is a little better there; then, when there appears to be a little better price from the British market they direct our live cattle there, with the result that we find ourselves left, as we were for a few weeks last winter, in a position where it is difficult to find any market at all. We believe that if we could develop a continuous market in the old country, it would be to the advantage of our cattle people to do so. At the moment we are experimenting to convince ourselves one way or the other on the facts; we think at the moment that if we had facilities established along the route to have our cattle slaughtered on this side and shipped across in substantial amounts, and had the facilities to handle them, we could satisfy the old country market and keep it to better advantage than we are doing, and under those circumstances we hope we shall get a price which will warrant our producers in keeping our cattle in that market.
The matter of facilities is not the only problem which has to be dealt with. If it were merely a case of slaughtering cattle in connection with the experiment at Saint John, and knowing we could always do that to advantage, we might conduct the experiment entirely from Saint John. But if we are to continue to gather our cattle at the centres where we have gathered them in the past, Toronto will need to be given consideration, because the greatest volume of our best cattle comes to the Toronto market, and unless strong reasons could be supplied for an individual taking them to some point further east they would continue to go to Toronto, and under certain conditions might find their way back as far as the Buffalo or Chicago market when we might prefer to see them going to Britain. That is the reason for including Toronto for the time being in the experiment, whatever the result of it may be.
As far as the production of the cattle themselves is concerned, I stated to the house last year and, I think, in the preceding year, that we were hopeful of developing some plan of inducing the movement of many of our young cattle from areas in western Canada where we cannot maintain them. We can
breed the verj' best of cattle and bring them up to a year or eighteen months under conditions which keep them in the very best possible health and produce the very best kind of feeder, but in many seasons we have not the feed with which to finish the cattle. We have been attempting to develop a natural movement of cattle from the west towards the east, to be fed on grass and in stalls in the eastern part of Canada and moved in the end to what we consider one of our natural markets, namely the British market. At the moment we are trying to associate the construction of community pastures in western Canada with that policy. We are organizing those pastures in areas where some attention has already been given to the breeding of live stock, largely through the fact that they are in natural ranching areas, and we are hopeful of having a policy in connection with breeding, especially in relation to pastures which have an acreage of twenty to one hundred thousand acres, that will bring out of those pastures a common type of stock. It can be said then to any community in eastern Canada, " Well, if you want to obtain the very best type of shorthorn feeders-or whiteface feeders, or the type my hon. friend is interested in, Aberdeen-Angus feeders-there are certain of those areas where that is the .type which is 'bred, and by sending there you can get that type of cattle. Even without going for them, you can get so many carloads of that particular type of cattle shipped down to your area." We are hopeful, through the development of that policy over a term of years, that we can accomplish what they have accomplished in the Argentine because of their close proximity to the sea; we can get those cattle moved eastward and have them down here at a year old; probably they can go on the grass for a year, or they may be stall fed for a winter. If we can induce our friends in the townships of Quebec to feed more 'beef cattle; if we can persuade our friends in the Saint John valley to feed more beef cattle, and our friends in Nova Scotia to do the same, we can bring cattle down and perhaps in some of those areas they can produce the feed to finish them. If they can not produce feed they can ship it in to better advantage than we in the west, who have not the same facilities in respect of water transport. If our experiment proves successful and we can market fresh killed beef in Britain to advantage, facilities can be provided by cooperative organ1 zations, the government, or private organizations- whoever will take an interest in it-to place that beef on the market in competition with beef coming from the Argentine and elsewhere.
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
Could the minister tell us approximately the quantity he has in mind in his reference to definite quantities of fresh killed beef?
Twenty-five carcases a week constitute the quantity under consideration at the moment.
And that arrangement is carried on through the government, not by private individuals?

The arrangements would be carried on through an agreement entered into by the government with any of the private organizations that desire to undertake it. Up to date there are only two that have indicated the desire to do so-Canada Packers and Swifts. But the government only pays any losses that may be incurred. If the beef does sell .to advantage after being shipped, in all probability the government will not have to pay anything, but if there are any losses in connection with it the government will pay the losses.

The minister was in Nova Scotia last year. I think he opened the maritime winter fair in Amherst. Has he anything to say regarding the opportunities of Nova Scotia for raising cattle for the British market? I know my county has fine beef cattle. They tell me that the exhibition at Bridgewater exhibits the finest show of beef cattle that one can see anywhere in eastern Canada. It seems to me Nova Scotia should be able to raise cattle for the British market. We have plenty of pastures, the very best, similar to those in Scotland. The abundance of dew and rain makes the pastures green and the grass grow quickly, and I cannot understand why we cannot in Nova Scotia, with our geographical position, raise cattle which will be acceptable on the British market.

The natural conditions in Nova Scotia, of course, are favourable, but the fact remains that that province does not produce nearly as many cattle as it might, largely, I suppose, because that market has not been properly developed and the means of getting the cattle there have not been properly developed. But I would point out that, while the conditions in certain parts of Nova Scotia compare favourably with those in Scotland, the Scottish people do not attempt to raise all the cattle they feed. The main part of the industry of producing feeder cattle which we now carry on is in order to supply the Scottish feeder with feeders. When I was in Glasgow two years ago I was talking to a very large feeder who feeds cattle in the
IMr. Gardiner.]
vicinity of St. Andrews, Scotland. He said that he had seven farms; that he and his two sons were in the market buying Canadian cattle, and that up to the time I was speaking to him he had bought thirty. I asked him how many Canadian cattle he could take. This was in the month of August. He said, "Between now and November I can take six hundred, if I can get six hundred like the thirty I have just bought," and he said he had not any idea that he would get more than a fraction of that number in the period, by coming down to Glasgow and picking up what he could get.
Would it be impossible to get twenty-five a week of the right quality in the maritime provinces?

I am not sure whether it would be possible to get twenty-five a week of the type they want. We want to keep a certain type on the market for one year and then be able to assure the British people that we can produce afteiwards a certain number of the same type. By that method it might be possible to induce some one to take an interest in that kind of trade.
We have good beef cattle.
The cattle I saw there were as good as one could find anywhere. I saw some later at the royal fair and they took prizes.

Seeing that there are good cattle in the maritimes, a small shipment might have been tried from that section, which is close to ,the British market. The minister has suggested that those who ship the twenty-five head weekly will be reimbursed for any loss, and naturally, if they make a profit, that is their inducement to cooperate with the government. I take it that the government will have a careful inspection made, because it is only under government inspection that any type should be allowed to be exported by the private individual. What I mean is this: H the department is reimbursing the private shipper for any loss that may be sustained, its inspectors should select the carcases that are exported. I assume that will be the procedure.

Yes. The department
will have a check on that all the way through. In Canada we have established over the years certain methods of marketing and I do not know whether we can change them, but for the time being our cattle are being exported in great numbers from certain points. Our main desire is to determine whether we can

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
set up conditions under which we can constantly divert a certain number of these to the British market. Personally I think we should be sending about 200,000 to the British market, and we should maintain that number. If we could send that number to the British market and the same number to the United States, carefully selecting them from certain sections, it would assist materially in building up our trade. But a constant level must be maintained. As it is one year we ship 6,000, another year 60,000, and if we go ten years back we find that in one year we shipped 100.000 and sometimes 200,000. These variations are such that we cannot say we are maintaining any position in the British market. What we should assure ourselves of is that even with present marketing conditions, with the great bulk of the stock being accumulated at Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg, we can go ahead and compete in the British market. If we can do that, then we shall have conditions under which we can compete to better advantage.

The principle involved in this experimental service in connection with beef cattle is of great importance, and it is one that could be put into effect to great advantage in connection with other lines of exports, particularly animal products. I do hope that the department will see that the quantities we ship are of sufficiently high quality. It would be in the interests of the great bacon industry of Canada if similar precautions were taken to maintain the quality of bacon shipped overseas. We have such an enormous market in Canada that those who are interested in the processing of live stock products here are bidding to the most important market, the one that takes ninety or ninety-five per cent of the product. Only a very small fraction is shipped overseas, and the price which is received for that surplus automatically fixes the price for the large quantity sold in Canada. Sometimes the large quantity sold here automatically in turn increases consumption in Canada, and as it increases consumption I am not sure that the individual processor does not make more money by selling high class products in Canada instead of looking for markets for a high class product overseas, which would automatically increase the price of the article to the farmer here. I suggest that not even bacon or other live stock products should be exported unless precautions are taken to see that a proper standard of inspection is maintained.
I commend the department for the experiment in connection with the shipment of twenty-five weekly, and I suggest that the
most careful system of inspection and supervision be carried out, independently of the ability of those who are processing. The integrity of those with whom the department is negotiating need not be questioned; but it is most important and fundamental it order to attain the end aimed at, namely a market for fresh beef overseas, that a system of careful inspection should be carried out. The same principle might very well be followed in connection with bacon and dairy products, and, indeed, practically all live stock products. As I say, the very small percentage that is exported automatically fixes the price for the whole dominion, and it is therefore of the utmost importance that this small percentage should be of high quality. It is only four or five per cent in the case of bacon, and in all animal products it is not ten per cent. It is extremely important that this surplus should be of a high quality which will bring a price that will reflect favourably on the price paid in Canada, which in many places is lower than cost of production.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, March 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Woods-worth for the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the criminal code.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): When this bill was before the house some time ago, Mr. Speaker, I indicated, as indeed the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) had stated previously, that the right of workers to form or join trade unions has the full support of this government. There is no difference whatever in that regard between us and the sponsor of this bill. There is in this measure, however, a very definite attempt to secure protection of the right to organize by an amendment to the criminal code, and it is the opinion of the law officers of the Department of Justice that such legislation would be colourable and that the proper means of giving due effect to freedom of association lie within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. In those circumstances, therefore, obviously the government cannot accept
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

legislation which, in .the opinion of the law officers of the crown, would be inoperative and invalid.
In this connection I wish to point out that on various occasions the dominion government has affirmed the right of workers to organize in trade unions; but it has always done so in the form of a declaration and has never proceeded by way of a legislative enactment. It may be interesting to members of the house to recall that the first formal declaration of this kind was made in the closing months of the great war. In July of 1918 an order in council was passed which was designed to bring about industrial peace in those difficult years. It was set out in that order in council that it would be in the interests of industrial peace that employers should give full recognition to the right of workers to organize. I should like to quote from the order in council a number of clauses which are pertinent to this discussion:
1.	That there should be no strike or lockout during the war.
2.	That all employees have the right to organize in trade unions, and this right shall not be denied or interfered with in any manner whatsoever, and through their chosen representatives should be permitted and encouraged to negotiate with employers concerning working conditions, rates of pay, or other grievances.
3.	That employers shall have the right to organize in associations of groups, and this right shall not be denied or interfered with by workers in any manner wrhatsoever.
4.	That employers should not discharge or refuse to employ workers merely by reason of membership in trade unions or for legitimate trade union activities outside working hours.
5.	That workers in the exercise of their right to organize shall use neither coercion nor intimidation of any kind to influence any person to join their organizations or employers to bargain or deal therewith.

speechtext: That was in 1918, so it would foe the union government of that day. The order in council is dated July 11, 1918.

But the point is that if it were passed by virtue of the authority of the War Measures Act it would have the
flV*r. Rogers.]
effect of law; otherwise it would be merely a pious declaration. If it were under the War Measures Act, of course it would last only until the War Measures Act was repealed some time later.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Yes. Well, I can say that in the preamble it does not appear that the order in council was passed under the provisions of the War Measures Act.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Does it not specify the act under the authority of which it was passed?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
No. Perhaps I should quote the preamble:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report dated 9th July, 1918, from the Minister of Labour, representing that industrial unrest during the past few months has become more general than formerly, thus causing serious interruption in some lines of war work, and indications are that it will become more widespread still unless successful efforts be made to check it. This unrest has many causes, among which are the shortage of labour, rapid advance in the cost of many of the necessaries of life, employers denying their workmen the right to organize or to meet them in joint conference to discuss requests for improved conditions or to negotiate adjustments of differences; and in others from too hasty action on the part of working men in ignoring the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and in adopting drastic measures before exhausting every reasonable effort to reach a satisfactory settlement. Wages alleged to be inadequate, together with length of the work day said to be too long, are among other frequent causes of such unrest.
Then1 it goes on to say:
The minister, therefore, recommends that the governor in council declare the following principles and policies and urge their adoption upon both employers and workmen for the period of the war.
So I think it is quite clear from the form of the preamble thiat the order in council was designed rather to be a declaration on the part of the government, and was not intended to have legal effect under the War Measures Act. But as I mentioned a moment ago, at the close of the war-

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: What would be the effect of these orders in council? Would they have any legal standing?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Oh, no. This was really
an appeal, with the authority of an order in council, to employers and workmen to observe these principles as laid down for the promotion of industrial peace, and my point is that when the government has dealt with this question in the past it has proceeded by way of declaration and not by way of legislative enactment.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
At the close of the war these principles remained in effect as a declaration of the position of the dominion government towards recognition of the right of workers to organize in trade unions, but I have no doubt that on the part of a great many people of this country they were soon forgotten. I suppose it is natural that questions regarding the right to organize and collective bargaining become more acute in a period of increasing prosperity. It is a matter of common knowledge that strikes are more frequent in such periods than during periods of depression. It so happened that shortly after this government came into office a number of strikes did occur, on account of charges that employers had been discriminating against some of their employees who belonged to trade unions. This government received a number of delegations from labour organizations in Canada, all emphasizing the importance of a more general recognition on the part of employers of the right of workers to organize in unions of their choice. When that matter was brought to the attention of this government and particularly to the attention of the Minister of Labour, who has a special interest and responsibility in these matters, the particular question of jurisdiction was referred to the law officers of the Department of Justice. That was in December, 1936. We were advised by the law officers of the Department of Justice that freedom of association was a civil right; that it lay within provincial jurisdiction, and that it was within the power of provincial legislatures to provide the means for a more adequate recognition of the right of workers to organize in trade unions.
In that connection I think I might very well remind the house that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, which had been particularly zealous in pressing this question upon the government, received legal advice, and on the basis of that legal advice had a bill drafted which was sent to all the provincial legislatures. I might quote from a circular letter from the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, addressed to the members of provincial legislative assemblies, and dated February 15, 1937. In that letter there is this paragraph:
Having secured legal advice we are informed that under the division of legislative powers between the dominion and the provinces the subject matter of this bill falls within the exclusive legislative competence of the provinces.
With that circular letter went this draft bill which was intended to secure, through provincial legislation, more adequate safeguards for workers who desire to form or to join trade unions.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Would the minister not say that was because of the attitude of the Department of Justice in saying the matter was provincial and not federal?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I have already stated to the house that on this question being referred to the Department of Justice, the Department of Labour was advised that the jurisdiction lay properly with the provinces. That view was communicated to the officials of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
At the same time there is clearly a suggestion here that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada themselves secured legal advice, and were advised accordingly that they should seek to Have their draft bill enacted by provincial legislatures rather than by the dominion parliament. I am sure the hon. member would not for one moment suggest that the law officers of the Department of Justice would not give a proper opinion in this case. They were asked for their opinion upon the case as submitted, knowing full well that the proposal had been made by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada
The opinion as given was communicated to the Trades and Labour Congress. They, I believe, took additional legal advice. Pursuant to that advice they later made representations to the provincial legislatures. I would add further that as a result of their representations to the provincial legislatures statutes have been passed in five provinces which, in effect, do provide additional safeguards for the rights of workers to organize in trade unions. In much of that legislation

and I shall not deal with it in detail because it was referred to previously by the Minister of Justice-there are special safeguards against employers who discriminate against their workmen because of membership or activity in trade unions.
I should like also to point out to the house that this government has at the same time done what it could properly do by declaration and persuasion to bring about, on the part of employers, a more general recognition of the right to organize. On January 1, 1937, as Minister of Labour I issued a statement which had behind it the full approval and endorsement of the government, a statement which referred specifically to the importance, in the interests of industrial peace, of a clear recognition on the part of employers of the right of their workers to organize in trade unions. Perhaps hon. members would permit me to quote briefly from that message:
In connection with recent strikes in Canada there have been frequent complaints that certain employers have denied to their employees
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

the right of association and have summarily discharged men and women who have been active in the organization of labour unions. It is necessary to state in the clearest terms that the right of association is a civil right, long established by law and usage. It was affirmed with special reference to Canada by an order in council of July 11, 1918 (P.C. 1743). It was proclaimed explicitly in the treaty of Versailles at the close of the world war. To deny the right of workmen to combine in any lawful organization they desire for the promotion of their common welfare is an open invitation to extremists to preach the futility of collective bargaining as an alternative to direct action. The right of association for legitimate purposes should be respected in the national interest and labour should not be denied the means of organizing for collective bargaining. The right of employers to organize for all lawful purposes is not questioned in any quarter. Employers are not entitled in the same breath to protest against governmental regulation of industry and to deny to labour its right to resort to legitimate measures of self-help through voluntary association.
I quote that simply to indicate to the hon. member, if indeed, it is necessary, that there has been no hesitation on the part of this government to do what it properly could to secure a more general acknowledgment of the right of workers to organize in trade unions. During the past two years I have had occasion to repeat that declaration on numerous occasions. May I say further that there have been a number of cases where employers are alleged to have discharged their employees because of their connection with trade union activities. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) referred specifically to a number of these cases when he spoke upon the bill. Whenever such cases have been brought to the attention of the Department of Labour we have done what we could by way of persuasion, and with the full influence of the government behind that persuasion to induce employers to reinstate workmen who have been discharged for such causes. I shall not say to the house that we have been uniformly successful in securing the reinstatement of workers discharged under these circumstances. At the same time I have been agreeably surprised at the attitude of a number of employers who apparently did not realize the fact that in discharging their workmen for such causes they were entrenching upon the freedom of association and were violating a civil right which, after all, is one of those civil rights which make up our heritage of freedom.
I can equally assure the house that this government-and I am not suggesting other governments have not also been active in this respect-will not cease to use its efforts in that direction.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: What recourse has an individual who is discharged and is not taken back?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
The truth of the matter is that prior to the passage of the legislation in the last two years by provincial legislatures, to which I referred a moment ago, there was no recourse. The situation was then very unsatisfactory. I fully agree with the hon. member in that regard. The most that could be done before that legislation was passed was to point out to employers that they had violated a civil right, and that they should take immediate steps to make amends for what they had done. As I have stated, in a very considerable number of cases reinstatements were brought about in that way. Of course, there is always the question as to how one can best encourage and bring about a more general acceptance of freedom of association, and a more general realization of the advantages of collective bargaining.
In supporting the bill the hon. member referred to legislation in other countries and, as I recall it, referred in particular to the Wagner Act passed by the United States congress. It is possible, where jurisdiction has been established, to deal with this matter in a manner which will compel employers to deal with trade unions, and through processes of collective bargaining. In the United States that legislation is of quite recent origin. It has been declared valid by the supreme court, because of the very wide powers conceded to congress through its control of interstate commerce.
In another country, a country from which Canada has inherited the greater part of her tradition, the question has not been dealt with upon the basis of coercion. In Great Britain there is no legislation of the nature of the bill now before the house. Among the employers of Great Britain there has developed over a period of years recognition of the value of collective bargaining. The right to organize, or what we term freedom of association, has been supported by an educated public opinion. I certainly hope that in this country there will be an increasing measure of support for the processes of collective bargaining. To my mind, if you can establish trust and good faith between employers and employees in the conduct of their industrial relations, you have established what is by far the best basis for industrial peace. In other words, it is desirable that these practices should develop, where possible, upon a voluntary basis. That has been the way in which the practice of collective bargaining has developed in Great Britain. I believe there is reason to hope that we are moving more and more in that direction in Canada.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
I have no fault whatever to find with my hon. friend for submitting this bill to the house. As a matter of fact, I think he is to be commended for emphasizing the importance of this question. However, I know he will not misunderstand me when I say that in the light of the advice given by the law officers of the Department of Justice it would be in the nature of deception upon those whom my hon. friend is anxious to assist if this government gave its support to legislation which, it is considered, would be invalid and inoperative. I cannot emphasize too strongly the support which I feel should be given to this right to organize. I want to express once more my own conviction that within the last few years there has been a marked improvement on the part of employers in their attitude toward this important question and in their relations with their employees.

I believe the answer to
that question would be that the right to organize is a civil right. On several occasions the dominion government has gone as far as it could go, under the advice of its law officers in affirming that right and in giving its full support' to the freedom of workers to organize in unions.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to observe, from what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) said, that the government has a good deal of sympathy for the proposal now before the house. However, I think the house ought to take a more definite attitude toward this question and not bring in the British North America Act as a sort of excuse for doing nothing. I use the words "sort of excuse," because I feel quite sure that if I were to go to lawyers in this chamber, even to those sitting on the Liberal side, I could get opinions to the effect that this bill is entirely intra vires of the British North America Act. I can remember in 1935 when we had the opinion of the law officers of the crown that certain measures then introduced were within the confines of the British North America Act. However, when they came before the highest court in the empire it was found that the law officers of the crown were not quite correct. The same thing might happen in this particular case.
I have seen lawyers in the courts and other places arguing cases. One lawyer would have in front of him a stack of precedents about two feet high in favour of his side of the case,
while the other .would have just as high a stack of precedents in the opposite direction. It is the easiest thing in the world for a lawyer to dig up precedents to show why something is either right or wrong.

speechtext: You have no idea now hard it is.

speechtext: They charge $100 a day to do it.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: I think it is one of tne easiest things in the world to dig up precedents. I shall go so far as to say that it may be a little difficult for some lawyers to dig them up.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada were most active in promoting legislation of this kind, even before this bill was introduced. Does my hon. friend not think they would have satisfied themselves on the legal question before they submitted the draft bill to the provincial legislatures?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
I can deal right away with the question asked by the hon. minister. The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada suggested in a circular submitted to the various provincial councils which were affiliated with them, that this matter came within provincial jurisdiction, but I understand that before that circular was sent out they consulted with members of the government. It was probably on the say-so of members of the government that they took the attitude they did. However, I have before me the statement they submitted to the Rowell commission in January, 1938, and from this it would appear that they have had a change of heart on this important question. This is what they submitted to the commission:
Where social and labour matters are concerned, the effect of the series of judgments of the privy council on the British North America Act has been to declare for provincial jurisdiction with rare exceptions because such subjects were held to be matters of civil rights and hence provincial. Without presuming to question the soundness in law of the decisions, it can be pointed out that the entire course of those judgments might just as well have taken an opposite direction in so far as the opinions of the judicial committee are concerned. We base this statement on two important principles laid down by the privy council itself in dealing with our constitution. The first of these principles was given in a decision of 1896 (the Distillers and Brewers' case) when their lordships stated that they did not doubt "that some matters, in their origin local and provincial, might attain such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion and to justify the Canadian parliament in passing laws for their regulation or abolition in the interests of the dominion." Obviously this means that a matter of civil
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

rights or of a local or private nature in its origin should cease to be reserved exclusively to the provinces when it becomes of such prominence to attain national significance.
I am not a lawyer, but I venture to assert that this particular judgment can be interpreted to mean that the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) comes entirely within the category to which reference is made.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: That judgment would be before the law officers of the Department of Justice when they gave their opinion on this question.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
The minister referred to the submission of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and I was giving this as part of their submission to the Rowell commission, after the circular referred to had been sent out. This indicates clearly that they felt that matters of this kind, which would pertain to the bill now before the house, would come within the scope of that interpretation and, therefore, within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament.
Again this year, in 1938, the year the Trades and Labour Congress submitted the same request to the dominion government. Let me read it:
We realize that jurisdiction in these matters rests with the provinces at present, rather than with parliament, and in the past year we have approached the several legislatures seeking protective legislation, with success in some cases. We firmly believe, however, that the dominion parliament also should recognize the rights of the workers to freedom of association and collective bargaining in as far as its jurisdiction extends, by providing suitable penalties for proven cases of interference with those rights.
That is the last word which the Trades and Labour Congress submitted to the cabinet in the early part of this year. Then, in January of this year, as previously mentioned, it submitted to the Rowell commission the following, which is also to be found on page five of its submission:
The second principle, contained in the decision on the radio case (1932), may be taken either as an extension of the first, or as parallel to it. Lord Dunedin, in giving judgment, had established that the point at issue was given by the act neither to the dominion nor to the provinces. As a residual power, and as a matter essentially national, jurisdiction was declared to rest with the federal authority.
I declare that the matter dealt with in the bill now before us is of such dimensions that it has become federal in its scope and nature and if the federal parliament enacted the legislation I believe it would be difficult to have it declared ultra vires and beyond the powers of parliament under the British North America Act.

Really the question would
have to be decided by the courts. I have not gone to any lawyers to obtain an opinion on the bill; but personally, from my own reading and having studied the matter as well as a layman can, I believe it is clearly within the jurisdiction of parliament to enact legislation of this kind.
I would say, further, that in the attitude which parliament has adopted in years gone by in regard to the jurisdiction of parliament and of the provinces we have been stirring up for ourselves a pile of trouble until we have reached an impasse, and now we do not know where we stand and where jurisdiction lies, whether with the federal parliament or with the provincial legislatures, with respect to various matters.
But matters pertaining to trades unionism and the right of workers to organize, and any penalties in relation thereto, are, in my opinion, purely federal, because, after all, trade and industry are matters of federal concern. You can not have one right in one province and another right in another province; and on the further ground of the desirability and the necessity of having uniformity in such matters I think a bill of this kind would be entirely within the scope of the federal parliament.
It has been claimed by the Minister of Labour that there are certain employers of labour who have denied to their employees the right to organize; that the employees who have organized have been penalized for attempting to become part of what one might call a legitimate trade union in Canada. If no penalty is provided for such employers of labour, then the right to organize becomes a mockery. In fact, the workers have not this right. Within recent times, within the last six months or so, we have had this right demanded by workers all across this dominion. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Madnnis) cited the case of Burns and Company at Vancouver, and a few weeks ago I referred to the employees of the Canadian Press who were being denied at that time the right to collective bargaining and the right, in many respects, to be recognized as a union. Illustrations galore could be given of men being intimidated and of ordinary

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
men and women being denied this right. The employee is not in the same fortunate or favourable position as the employer of labour.
The Minister of Labour referred to conditions in Great Britain. I think he knows more about the history of the trades union movement and more about the struggle of the masses in Great Britain than I ever knew. But there is a history attached to the growth of the trades union movement and the labour movement in Great Britain, and when the minister says it grew gradually by a process of mutual understanding between employers and employees, I do not think he was putting the case quite correctly. We in this country are years behind Great Britain in these matters. I am not now referring to the Trades Union Act of 1906 because, even if that were not in existence in Great Britain, we are still a long way behind that country in the scope of our trades union activities. One of the reasons why to-day there is in Great Britain more of this mutual understanding between employer ad employee is because the trades unions have grown in strength over a period of years until they have become so strong that they have not only earned the respect of employers of labour but also inspired them with fear.
There is a different situation in Great Britain from that which prevails in Canada at the present time. Here in the past few years we have been turning back the hands of the clock. Look at the recent legislation passed in the province of Quebec. Surely the hand of progress has been going backward during the past few years. One has to go back almost a century and a quarter to find a parallel. To show how the British trades union movement has developed, I might cite the famous Times case which was decided in 1812, under the Combination Act of 1799. Men who had tried to organize were found guilty and were sentenced to terms of imprisonment ranging from nine months to two years. This is what the judge said to the prisoners in the dock on that occasion, in 1812:
Prisoners, you have been convicted of a most wicked conspiracy to injure the interests of those very employers who gave you bread; with intent to impede and injure them in their business and indeed as far as in you lay to effect their ruin.
The frequency of such crimes among men of your class of life and their mischievous and dangerous behaviour to ruin the fortunes of those employers, which a principle of gratitude and self interest should induce you to support, demands of the law that a severe example should be made of those persons who shall be convicted of such daring and flagitious combinations in defiance of public justice and in
defiance of public order. No symptom of contrition on your part has appeared, no abatement of the combination in which you are accomplices has yet resulted from the example of your convictions.
That is going back about 125 years, or a little more, and if we look at the history of the trades union movement we find its inception dates back to about that particular period. When they found that industrial activity was not sufficient to give them what they wanted in those days they turned to political action, and from political action they turned to industrial action. So, gradually, over a period of years there has grown in Great Britain the industrial and the political movements which to-day have become such a powerful factor for progress in the old country. It might be of interest to note the demands of the Chartist movement, which barely 100 years ago first became prominent in what one might call British democracy. What were its famous demands? One was equal electoral areas; the second, universal suffrage; the third, payment of members; the fourth, no property qualification; the fifth, vote by ballot; the sixth annual parliaments. To-day these demands look picayune because of the progress we have made over the years. If I may advance over a period of time and come down to the time when the Independent Labour party of Great Britain was born, they formulated a program which to-day looks so conservative and limited that one is inclined to express surprise at the timidity of those who formulated it less than half a century ago. There are many to-day who can still remember the formation of the British Independent Labour party. I myself have a very faint recollection of it.

They asked for the abolition of child labour under fourteen years of age; a legal eight hour maximum working day; state provision for the aged, sick and disabled workers and for widows and orphans; abolition of indirect taxation and taxation to extinction of all unearned incomes, and work for the unemployed-every proposal for the purpose of extending political rights and democratizing the system of government. My hon. friend knows how these efforts expressed themselves in the repeal of the Taff Vale judgment and the passing of the Trades Union Act of 1906. These things occurred because of the growing strength of the organized labour movement in Great Britain. And when, in 1918, the government of the day in Canada passed an order in council which stated that the workers had the right to organize, and contained other beneficial provisions, it was done at a time when labour was in the ascendency in this country and when the need for labour and for peace in industry was most urgent. It is not my intention to intrude myself into this debate, but there have come to the fore one or two questions upon which I thought it my duty to make an observation or two.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in a remark attempted to convey the idea that progressive reforms in England were instituted by the Liberal party and its adherents. I would invite the minister in his spare moments to review his British history and see whether he cannot satisfy himself that most of the reforms which were introduced into England from 1832 to the present time were brought forward by Conservatives and embodied in Conservative legislation. I do not need to particularize; but it will be recalled, for instance, that the two reforms of the electoral law were instituted by British Conservative governments, and the same is true of child labour legislation. I make that remark merely by way of correction. If we come to our own country we shall find that Conservatives have been in no way behind Liberals in introducing reform measures. The right hon. gentleman might recall to mind, among others, enactments of very recent date which prove that the Conservatives made at least a real effort to put on the statute books and give effect to legislation beneficial to the workers and intended to improve social conditions in this country.

I do not want to delay the item unduly, but in view of what I said this afternoon, and having regard to the information that grew out of the discussion, I feel that I must reiterate what I said. Though I am sure t'he minister is actuated by the best intentions in the world, I believe he is off on the wrong foot. I suggest that we should give this project a 100 per cent test. We have had undertakings to place on the British market the product which I mentioned, fresh-killed meat. The minister gave us a certain amount of information this afternoon, when he told us that in the experiment conducted by the university of Saskatchewan meat processed at Montreal fetched a little lower price than British killed meat. Then he told us that meat processed at Saskatoon fetched still less than that processed at Montreal. It seems to me that if we would go just a little further and process this meat right at the Atlantic seaboard, we would have a chance to place this product in the British market in such a way that it would perhaps fetch a price equal to that paid for the home killed product itself.
The minister also told us that the government were to reimburse the packers for any loss they might sustain in this experiment. I want to say in all sincerity that I think the government would be well advised to go just a little further. There must 'be abattoirs on the Atlantic coast, at Halifax and Saint John; perhaps they are owned by the same people. Why not have this meat processed on the
