Atlantic coast, as I have suggested, and give it that final and the only sure and fair test? So my suggestion to the minister is that in the interests of Canada and of this great industry we should do everything within our power to place the best possible product on the market that we hope to enter.

I should like to refer to the statement made by the minister two or three hours ago, that we in the west should raise cattle and send them to the east coast for finishing. I have been wondering why we could not make use of our own products; why we could not send our grain out in the form of beef rather than pay high freight rates and have to put that grain through the exchange at Winnipeg. I believe we could escape that evil at least by sending our cattle to the seaboard in a finished condition. In that way I believe quite an improvement would be brought about to the advantage of the western farmer. Another thing I believe we should do is provide a steady market for our cattle. I have before me the numbers of cattle that have been shipped to the United Kingdom and to the United States since 1928, and there has not been at all a steady flow.

With an irregular flow like this, I do not think it is possible to maintain a worthwhile market, and I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, who suggested that the government had an opportunity through this experiment to do something beneficial for the farmers of the west.

When I came in this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, the hon. the Minister of Agriculture was speaking of "live stock"; and I felt that while I was not in the category about which he was speaking, I was still alive, and to prove it I am now on my feet. I was struck by the remarks of the minister this afternoon in explaining this item, as I was by the remarks of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) who is leading
the opposition to-night in the regrettable absence of the right hon. the leader of the opposition, and by the interest shown by that hon. gentleman in the development of cattle raising and cattle exporting from the maritime provinces. It seems to me that Nova Scotia-and I speak more particularly of the constituency which I have the honour to represent together with my colleague the other member for Halifax- has not been as progressive in this matter as might be wished. It is not my duty to speak for the entire province, but I should like to explain my position and what I believe to be the position of the cattle raisers of Nova Scotia and more particularly of my own constituency. I wonder if I could obtain the figures as to the exports of cattle raised in the maritime provinces or Nova Scotia, to the British market, through the efforts and under the general policy of the Department of Agriculture?
Carried.

I am not being carried; I am still alive. I may be able to obtain that information later, but it is a regrettable fact that in our province, and in the county of Halifax more particularly, we are taking a retrograde step in reference to this item, which is a branch of agriculture. When you go to the agricultural fair up in the Musquodoboit valley, which is one of the most fertile spots in our lovely province, you see on exhibition some of the finest cattle that can be seen in any part of Canada. If you go to the provincial exhibition in the city of Halifax you will find the same thing. H you go to the various county fairs throughout the province, in those counties where cattle can be raised profitably if given a fair show, you will see cattle that will compare favourably with what is known as western steer beef. I heard the minister say this afternoon that he was interested in the same breed of cattle as that in which the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare was interested; I think it was the "Aberdeen-Angus." I do not know whether that is a mixture from Scotland and the premier of Nova Scotia, whose name happens to be "Angus" L. Macdonald. It does seem to me that the great obstacle, the great setback, the hindrance, to our people is largely due to the fact that the large corporations, such as Canada Packers, practically control the maritime market. They are not a great benefit in the city of Halifax or to the cattle breeders of the province. When tenders are called from persons engaged in the legitimate business of cattle raising and cattle

selling, these tremendous corporations, which sell directly to the wholesaler in Halifax and throughout Nova Scotia, tender also in competition. In nine cases out of ten the wholesaler is put to one side because Canada Packers would get the contract. The man in the wholesale business paying his income tax, his rent, his business tax, his city tax and his school tax, has to stand aside while this corporation, which has developed like the roots of the rubber tree in southern countries, obtains the business. Where those trees grow one cannot build a house, because once the roots of the tree are reached it is impossible to find the terra firma upon which to build, and the land in the neighbourhood of the tree must be abandoned as a possible site for building. If this sort of thing continues, agriculture in Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces will become a thing of the past.
Let me give one further illustration which, to my mind, is convincing beyond contradiction of even the most technical expert in agricultural matters. Eatons and Simpsons have come into the maritimes market in the city of Halifax. In construction Eatons spent about a million dollars. They bought out Mahon Brothers, one of the two leading retail general dry goods stores, one which had a splendid standing in the community, and developed a large business. The Eaton company paid its help less wages, and followed a practice of taking some of them on for two or three days and then laying them off for a similar period. In connection with their store a groceteria has been developed in which they display, to a degree of which only Eatons and Simpsons are capable, beef and other agricultural products. The displays are presented in such a manner that the people flock to the store. While buying other things, they visit the groceteria, and on Saturday, which is market day, they buy their beef, eggs butter and cheese in those departmental stores.
The matter has developed to such an extent that on one occasion I thought it well to speak to the premier, the Hon. Mr. Macdonald, on the point. I said to him that I thought the effect of that type of trade was against the interests of the agriculturists of the province, and particularly those in the vicinity of Halifax. I was not speaking politically. Most of those agriculturists are to the north, northeast and east of Halifax city, across the harbour, on the Dartmouth side. We know that in the vicinity of Cole Harbour there is fertile land suitable for the raising of cattle and poultry, or in the production of eggs which some day may develop into chickens. We find that the farmers come in to Halifax

from Cole Harbour, Eastern Passage, Cow Bay, Lawrencetown, East Chezzetcook, West Chezzetcook, Little River, Middle Musquodo-boit and Upper Musquodoboit. They used to come to the market and stand around on the sidewalks of what was known as Cheapside, opposite the post office. There they sold the products of their farms and did a splendid business. Rain or shine they were there, without cover. At that time an attempt was made by the city council to drive them out. I was serving in the legislature of Nova Scotia

I do not raise the point through any desire to speak about myself-but "Joe Howe" preserved to them their interminable right to cany on their trade there, and I placed legislation upon the statute books to permit them to continue to carry on their trade on these sidewalks. Later on, the city of Halifax built a market on Market street.
What is happening to-day? Those people are doing scarcely any business. The people who do buy from them wait until late Saturday afternoon so that they may get something for nothing. In fifty per cent of the cases the farmers carry back most of their produce to be fed to the animals. They come back with their pockets empty because they have been unable to sell what they had produced on their farms. This condition is due solely to the great corporations coming into the market and taking part in every business under the sun-of course they have not attacked the sun or the moon. The result is that not only have they brought fear to the hearts of the farmers but they have brought unhappiness to the farmers' homes. The resoluteness of the farmer is gradually dying; the young men and women are leaving the farms and going to the cities and towns, even at the risk of facing unemployment.
In speaking about western beef this afternoon the Minister of Agriculture said that "the markets were practically controlled by Toronto and Montreal." Why should they be controlled in that way? Why should provision not be made under this very item for quotas from those provinces which produce cattle of a kind suitable for shipment to the old country? If such provision were made, there would be some impetus given to that kind of business, a trade which through no fault of their own the farmers have permitted to fall by the wayside. Such provision would give them and those who came after them some encouragement to stay on the land, and not to go the cities and towns to seek a precarious livelihood. I said to the Premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Macdonald, that I thought there was one way of overcoming the difficulty,

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
and that was to put a heavy tax on corporations such as Eatons Limited and Simpsons Limited. My observations are not directed particularly against those two companies; I am referring to other companies as well which are driving the farmer out of business.
The old merchants of Halifax are a thing of the past. You may go along Barrington street or along Granville street outside Wood Brothers, and you will not find any of the old firms left. The only wholesale house doing a drygoods business in Halifax to-day is the house of J. & M. Murphy, which is one of the oldest and weathered the gale. When we think of those old merchant firms we think of Mr. T. E. Kenny, who was once a member of this chamber and an honoured citizen, and we think of Burns & Murray, Doull & Miller. I look back upon those old reliable firms which were carrying on when I was a boy; at that time also there were ten or twelve wholesale grocery merchants in Halifax, but only one or two have survived. They are gone. Our industries are gone. Two or three are left, but the rest have been taken holus-bolus to Montreal. That is not the cattle industry either.
I would say to the minister that if they had remained, cattle would be used, cattle would be bred and cattle would be purchased from our own farmers. I do not desire to take a sectional view of this matter; I want to consider it broadly. However, we are at the extreme east of this great dominion. This is the time when there are differences between the various provinces as to the question of jurisdiction under the terms of the British North America Act. A royal commission, at the head of which is Chief Justice Rowell, is now sitting to consider these matters. There is a great diversity of opinion among the provinces, and one of them has come before the commission and said, "No, we will give you no information." This is a critical time in the history of Canada, and the country is not being welded into a whole as it should be.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would point out to
the hon. member that he is not confining his remarks to the item before the committee which has to do with live stock and poultry.

I have all due deference for
your rulings, Mr. Chairman; but as I said once before, matters have been discussed which involved in their finality the very matter to which I am referring. If I am not in order, if I cannot extend my remarks to the ultimate goal and the ultimate finish, then let me say that while I have not gone the distance I might have gone, I believe I 51952-1891
have said sufficient to bring this matter to the attention of the committee, and the people whom I represent. I am on the right road, and I shall go the limit at the proper time when the order paper is clear and no question can be raised as to whether I am in order or out of order. I am looking to the ultimate results that can be achieved by a proper development under this item which has to do with live stock and poultry.
I have a suggestion I should like to make to. the minister and to the technical officers of his department. If it is possible to do so, a quota should be allowed to the farmers and poultry raisers in Nova Scotia. An officer of the department should go there to see what cattle would be acceptable to the markets of Great Britain or Europe, we should not forget that the nearest point of shipment is Halifax. I am not talking against the port of Saint John or the summer ports on the St. Lawrence river; I say this in order that our people may feel that some interest is being taken in their welfare. A survey should be made of the possibilities of these maritimes. I know the Minister of Agriculture is interested in this matter. He has assiduously and fearlessly addressed himself to the problems involved. Through personal contact he has kept in touch with the markets abroad. He has studied these problems in the best way possible, and I believe the matter is safe in his hands and in the hands of his technical advisers.
I submit that the people of the east, particularly those in Nova Scotia and in my own constituency, should foe given a chance. If they can produce live stock and poultry which come under this item, they should be allowed an export quota. If that were done, it would offer them considerable encouragement and would be better than any " back to the land " sign you could put up. It would illustrate that " back to the land " means something. The people on the land would be able to feel the coin in their pockets, and others would see possibilities of making a living by going back to the land.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the dissatisfaction that exists throughout the farming community in connection with the grading of hogs. The farmers who have been in the bacon hog business for years know a select hog better than do some of the graders. Some of them have been taking particular pains to feed and breed these hogs, but when they send shipments to the abattoirs they find that they have only one or two selects. There is a strong suspicion that some influence is brought
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

to bear upon the graders who are at the abattoirs all the time and that the farmers are not getting a square deal. I find this dissatisfaction existing all over the country. I know of one farmer who had a lot of some twenty-five bacon hogs. I looked at them and I judged that at least twenty were selects. They were Yorkshires and had been fed and bred in the proper manner. When this man got his return from the abattoir he found he had only three or four selects. Will the minister investigate this matter because I feel an injustice is being done to the producers of bacon hogs.

Just before the minister answers that question, may I say I was developing a point and I do not want to leave a wrong impression. I was referring to a conversation I had had with the premier of Nova Scotia in connection with imposing a tax. That tax was not to prevent the concerns to which I referred from doing business. The suggestion was that they should make a statement to the provincial secretary of the cattle and other farm products purchased in the province, and the tax would be lessened by the amount purchased to a minimum which would be fixed, and that would be the business tax.

What
progress has been made in the grading of hogs on the rail instead of on the foot?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
There are two methods of grading hogs; one is to grade them while they are still running around, and the other is to grade them after they have been hung up on the rail. It is much easier to grade them after they are on the rail because they can be fully examined. For a considerable number of years before I was in the department, it had been promoting the idea of rail grading. There was considerable opposition to this at first, as there is to any idea being introduced for the first time. However, there has been an increasing satisfaction with rail grading as compared with grading of the hogs while they are still alive. The figures indicate this growing satisfaction. In 1935 the number of carcases graded on the rail was 115,209; in 1936, 447,493; in 1937, 1,002,541. In those three years the figures have risen from 115,000 to over 1,000,000. Those are very satisfactory results, encouraging people at least to accept rail grading. It is much easier for any person to be satisfied with the grading when it has been done in that way.
But there has been objection taken to rail grading by those who are in the trade, and on occasion also by individuals; the objection is

based largely on the idea that our hogs are purchased mostly by private packers, and some people maintain that they would much prefer to have the hog graded while still running around and while they can dispose of it in some way, to having it hung up on the rail in a packer's plant and graded there. Rail grading has been developed to the highest point, I think, in Denmark where, as I said the other day, hogs are bred by the cooperative, in the first instance; where they are fed by the cooperative, and sold and marketed by the cooperative, the whole process right through being carried on in that way, and where that is done there is no difficulty in rail grading even up to 100 per cent. But here it is a case of persuading the people to accept rail grading as against the grading of the hog while still alive. I personally have had my own doubts. I sell some hogs from time to time from my own farm, and I do not know that I have been entirely satisfied that I got all the selects I should have received. I doubt very much if any of us are entirely satisfied with the grading of our live stock, or our grain, for that matter, unless we get top grade all the time. It is just possible, nevertheless, that there are some things which can be improved upon in connection with the grading, and an attempt is being made from time to time to make those improvements and to make it more easy to avoid mistakes, to put it mildly, in the grading, or an attempt on the part of some to take advantage of the fact that the farmer does not always know what the grade is.

I think the province
of British Columbia has not been considered a very heavy producer of swine, and there have been reasons for this in the past. One was the high cost of feed and other conditions that prevailed in some dairying districts, but of late years there has been a great effort made to revive and bring about an increase in the production of hogs. I was reading in the paper only to-day of one hog farmer in the lower mainland of the province who is producing about one thousand head a year, and another one about five thousand. But when one looks over the statistics one finds that we are importing into the province about 99 per cent of the ham and bacon we consume. The minister is aware of the fact that this industry is being organized on a large scale; that associations have been formed, and that a large number of farmers in the lower mainland of the province have joined these associations.
I notice that swine graders are being provided for in the item before us. Let me

Supply-Agriculture-M arkeling
remind the minister that during the last two or three months representations have been made to the live stock branch by the swine associations of the lower mainland for the appointment of a field man or a swine grader. I should like to know if the minister has taken that into consideration and if any provision will be made in the estimates to provide for such an official in that district?

Arrangements are being made at present to have a man established in British Columbia who will take charge of the grading of hogs in that province. That service was not previously given by the department in British Columbia; but the numbers produced, as has been indicated by the hon. member, have increased, and we feel now that we should give that service to the province.

Will this official be grading on the rail at the abattoirs or will he also act as a field man, so that the farmers could get some information on the type of hog they should raise and how to improve them?
The one man at that particular point will do both. He will grade in the stockyards on the hoof, and also grade in the packing plant on the rail.
Has the farmer any say at the present time as to how these hogs are graded? Can he have them graded on the rail or graded on the hoof as he desires?
It is for the farmer to decide whether they shall be graded on the hoof or on the rail.

When he sells to the drover, and the hogs go into the stock yard, has the farmer the right to say: "I want these graded on the rail," or "I want them marked," and then have them forwarded on as they are to the abattoirs?
It is a deal between the drover and the farmer. They can be graded on the rail if he makes that deal with the drover.
He has the option?
Yes.

I think every encouragement should be given to the farmer because if the dairy cow and the bacon hog in eastern Ontario are eliminated, the farmers would go bankrupt. Those are their greatest assets, and I am pleased to know that the minister is giving the matter his consideration and giving more thought to the grading of hogs.

With regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Halifax
(Mr. Finn) and the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) as to the number of cattle that can be shipped from Nova Scotia, I have the figures here from 1932 to 1936. Beginning with 1932, the number of cattle exported from Nova Scotia to all other markets was in that year 999; in 1933, 213; in 1934, 918; in 1935, 765; in 1937, 1.007. As to the number sold directly to the packers, I have not the figures for 1932 or 1933; but in 1934 the number was 1,275; in 1936, 102; in 1937, 370. That is, as the numbers exported went up, the numbers sold to the packers apparently went down. The grand total of cattle marketed in the different years, according to these figures, was in 1932, 240; in 1933, 212; in 1934, 2,210; in 1935, 955; in 1936, 1,409. As against that, store cattle were brought in, in 1933-I have not the figures for 1932-to the number of 36; in 1934, 64; in 1935, 46; in 1937, 1,365. It will be seen that the number of cattle brought in during 1937, 1,365, is about 100 less than the total number marketed through the packers or through export. This indicates that practically all of the cattle which are produced in the province of Nova Scotia are slaughtered locally and consumed locally.
How many were brought in from the drought area?

I should judge that most of them were, but that illustrates the point which was up this afternoon and again this evening. It would be very difficult to select 1,300 cattle from Nova Scotia to be shipped out, even under the test we are following, if we took all that were available. There has been only one year w'hen that number was shipped from Nova Scotia.
Why would that be?
The chief reason, I suppose, would be that they have been gradually going out of the production of cattle, and agriculture has been somewhat backward in the province from time to time.
Lack of markets.

But I do not know why that should be the case. My views about that are pretty much the same as those of the hon. member for Halifax. The people of Nova Scotia are located close to port. Some of the cheapest feed which can be found in the world can be shipped to Halifax at a lower price than it could be shipped anywhere else in Canada; even if they are not breeding cattle and producing them there themselves, I cannot see any reason why there could not be developed a good feeder industry in Nova

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
Scotia, and it is in the hope that we may be able to develop that industry that we have been encouraging the shipment of cattle from the west to Nova Scotia and to New Brunswick during the last few years. I think this figure for 1937 will be accounted for largely by the fact that we have been encouraging these shipments. The increase from a few hundred a few years ago to 1,409 last year is probably partly accounted for by that.

The minister said that the
figures he gave included shipments to Europe as well as -?
That is all the exports out of the province.

Not to any particular place. Then, might I ask the minister with reference to the 1,007 in 1937, an appreciable increase and pleasing to hear about. Were the cattle which were sent in for that purpose sent to people who were raisers of cattle in Nova Scotia, or did they go to special interests there?

I have not the figures before me as to how many cattle which went in under the special policy adopted two years ago are included in these figures, but a considerable number of cattle were purchased in the drought area of western Canada both for Nova Scotia and for New Brunswick in the fall of 1936 and again last year.

That is, by the agriculture
department?

No. The Department of Agriculture pays the fare of an individual from eastern Canada who wishes to purchase a carload or more in the west, and then the person purchasing the cattle comes back with the cattle; so that the fare of the individual is looked after in going west to buy cattle in the drought area. Then we paid one-half the freight provided the individual kept the cattle for three months and fed them; at the end of the three months we paid one-half the freight on the cattle shipped through. That was done particularly for the purpose of assisting people in getting rid of their cattle in the drought area and for the purpose of encouraging people in the far eastern part of Canada to import cattle from that area and become feeders of cattle.

Would it be possible to obtain from the statistical branch of the minister's department, as regards the 1,007 cattle that were shipped in 1937 from the drought area to Nova Scotia, who were the purchasers of those cattle, where the freight was paid or partly paid, the fare of the person who went

for them, where he came from and who he was, whether he was a farmer or just some person who went out like a cattle buyer or a horse buyer-they are sometimes called something else?

These figures can be
obtained. I have not them here with me this evening, but the information with regard to the individuals who purchased cattle and obtained payments can be furnished.

Thank you.
Mr. MacKENZIE (Lambton-Iient) I am not quite clear what the departmental rulings are with regard to the marking of hogs. Formerly a drover bought hogs from the farmer and graded them in the pen or the shipping yard before they left the shipping point. I believe that is still the practice in some places. The instructions which the department is now sending out are that each buyer must mark the hogs individually and make payment for the hogs on the basis of the official grading returns. This has caused a good deal of dissatisfaction in some places, and I want to know if that is the universal ruling of the Department of Agriculture or if it is simply applicable in some places.

The regulation is that all hogs have to be graded. If there is any doubt with regard to the grading, it can be required that the hogs be marked, and when they go to the central point they are regraded; but the general practice is that when the drover buys hogs he marks them, and there are very few people who raise complaints. The idea is that when he once takes them in at the central point they are his hogs; but the regulations require that if the person is not satisfied with the grading, he can have the grading checked.

The
understanding I have is that the department has sent out instructions to the buyers that they must mark all these hogs separately, individually, before they leave the shipping point, and they are paid for on the basis of the official grading returns as they are killed in the abattoir.

I understand there is some difficulty from time to time, and I am informed there has been some in the area from which my hon. friend comes; but my information is that wherever difficulties of that kind have arisen

and it applies to the case in question

the department has insisted that these hogs be marked, and that has been done in at least some cases in the area to which he has referred.

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
Would the minister consider the advisability of a regulation to have all hogs graded on the rail, in the interests of the export end of it and in the interests of the hog industry generally?

We have considered the advisability of it. We have not felt that public opinion is sufficiently behind it to warrant doing it at this time. When we are convinced that the public are ready we shall, of course, be prepared to make any further provision necessary.
The department more or less agrees that this is the more efficient way?
Yes; the department agrees that it is the more efficient way.

Regarding hog grading, I might say it was customary for the drover to grade the hogs, but one can understand that the drover gets in wrong with a great many of his customers if they think they have not as many selects as they should have; the majority of the drovers do not care to grade these hogs when they buy them, so they are marked and sent on to the abattoirs, where the government grader grades them, but the raisers of the hogs have to wait until the next shipment before the drover gets back his returns and pays them $1 apiece for their selects.
I see by this item that there are senior swine graders, swine graders and junior swine graders, and I should like to know the difference between them. There are three senior swine graders, fourteen swine graders, and twenty-five junior swine graders, and they are all paid different salaries. What is the difference?

The names applied to them describe pretty clearly what the difference is. The junior man is the man with the least experience; he has not as great a responsibility as the senior. The junior has the least experience, the swine grader next, and the senior swine grader is the most experienced.
There is an impression in our part of the country that the premium of $1 a hog is not large enough to encourage the farmers to produce the proper type of bacon hog.
The amount now is SI a hog.

What control, if any, is exercised over the differential in the different grades of hogs? It is -true that the premium for select hogs is $1; but when you get light hogs, even if they are the right type and the proper conformation, sometimes there is a
differential between the bacon price and the price of the live hog; and similarly with heavy hogs. Sometimes the differential is quite large. In some instances this creates a certain amount of dissatisfaction in the minds of the farmers. Does the department exercise any control in that regard?
The only control is in the matter of the premium of $1. As regards other differentials in other grades, that is a matter of agreement between the buyer and the seller.
What progress is being made in the grading of beef? I understand that an attempt is being made to grade beef and to have certain grades established.
There are two established grades, and in British Columbia, in three cities, they are establishing four. Those are compulsory. There are two optional grades established by the federal government.

I know there are two grades of beef, different labels, but I want to know what progress is being made by the department towards the universal grading of beef. Is any attempt being made to make it countrywide?

The question of expansion has been considered from -time to time. What is now being done in British Columbia is only an experiment, and if it works successfully it probably will be more widely applied across Canada.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to this debate, and to me it is wonderful the number of friends the dear farmer has in this house. If the farmer is not doing the drover, the drover is doing the farmer; but for my part I have never yet seen a farmer that anybody could do, and except for the last three or four years I have been dealing with them for thirty or forty years. If ever I was trimmed it was by a farmer, because I have always watched the business man or the dealer, but I never thought of watching the farmer. That is why I got trimmed.
Who watches you?

If you try to trim me, I may try to trim you; but if you give me a square deal I will give you one. I am willing at all times to make contributions or grants or subsidies to the farmers in order to assist the country, because without happy, contented farmers we cannot be happy; but I do not want to make the farmer so helpless that he will not be able to do anything at all for himself. If we go on in this way, doing,
298S
Supply-Agriculture-M arketing

necessary work for everyone, I am afraid we shall become a nation of imbeciles who will not be able to think for themselves, and that is bad policy.
I congratulate the hon. member for Halifax upon the remarks he made in regard to conditions in that old city which I knew so well years ago. There were quite a number of respectable wholesale houses there, but they were driven out by the chain store system. In my opinion, that system has done more to ruin the country than anything else. It is the same with big combinations of packers. They will drive out ten or fifteen wholesale business firms, respectable businessmen of high integrity, and they will do it ruthlessly. They steal all the business they can from everyone. I have absolutely no use for the chain store system, and in my opinion the government should have taxed them $1,000 for every store in Canada over one store in any city or town. If that were done, the country would be much better off. Money used to flow freely through everyone's hands; but to-day it is confined to a few, and it is in the control of big packers and the big interests. You can blame governments and no one else for this condition. You can talk until you are crazy and you will not get governments to take action.
What has that to do with the marketing of live stock and poultry?
It applies to the marketing of beef, which the Minister of Agriculture is trying to assist.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order is not well taken.
I understand that the minister is trying to assist in building up a market for meat killed in Canada and shipped to the old country. Is that right?
Yes.

I endorse all that, but I will not endorse the establishment of a big abattoir at Halifax or Saint John, because I know something about abattoirs. I was in the city council of Toronto once and we established one. It was said that it would reduce the cost of living, and the city of Toronto paid from $50,000 to $200,000 a year loss. That is what will happen in connection with this proposal. No doubt the minister will agree with the abattoir that they should take over the offal, and they will get a considerable sum from that. They will get a good deal of money from the hides and so on.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

No; sit down. To-day there is a duty of 3^ cents a pound on animal fat going into the United States. Fat here is very cheap and still we are bringing in vegetable oil free. I am afraid that if we get mixed up in the running of an abattoir, no one will know what the loss will be. It is suggested that the farmers should be reimbursed for their loss, but who will say what the loss is? If you kill twenty-five or fifty head of cattle and ship the product to the old country, every farmer who owned any of the cattle would demand compensation for loss. I submit that those who are charged with the responsibility of handling public money should handle it as carefully as their own. If the department is endeavouring to obtain the highest possible price for a farmer's cattle, expending the country's money in that effort, then I think he ought to be ready to take a chance too, and has no right to be reimbursed. It seems to me that we are getting more and more to the stage where apparently no one is fit to do his own business. Even men who think themselves smart are advocating that sort of thing in this house.
As I say, I am willing to do anything within reason to assist the farmer. In fact, I have made my living off the farm and you will not find any man in the province of Ontario who will say that I ever gave the farmer anything but a square deal. So I do not want it said that I am criticizing money spent to help build up business between here and the old country, because that is where we should build up our business, and not so much between Canada and the United States. I think we should pay less attention to the United States, because it is a most unstable market. They will take your goods for a week or so, if they need them; then, overnight, when you are caught at the border, they will put on an embargo or, if they do not put it on, they will ask the railways to do so. I remember that once, some years ago, I went to Winnipeg to buy ten carloads of western potatoes to be shipped to the United States. I had three carloads at the border, I think it was near Detroit, when I wired my son in regard to the potato market in the United State?. He wired me at once to get away from the potato market, that the United States had gone hooey and there was no market for potatoes, so I was stuck with those potatoes at the border. That is the way in which the United States does business, and we should treat them in the same way. We are not looking after ourselves in this country at all; we are just hewers of wood and drawers of water, raising families and educating them in this country, then sending them to the United States to build

Supply-Agriculture-M arketing
up industry there. That is what we have been doing for many years, but now they do not want our people any more. They did take our best educated people, however, for many years, and we kept this country poor educating them. In Canada we have men equal to those anywhere in the world; you cannot get better. I do not want to start saying that our people are so much better than those in other countries, but they are a very high type of people, and we do not realize just how good we are.
What about poultry?

I do not know anything
about poultry, so I am not going to talk about it. But I do know something about abattoirs; I was for some time chairman of the abattoir committee of the city council of Toronto; I visited that abattoir every day for two years and saw what was going on. It was an absolute mess, and if you get into that business you will get into another mess. Let somebody run the abattoir who knows how to run it, and if you can, tie him up so that he cannot do anything wrong. That will be difficult, however, if you are dealing with Canada Packers, because I have no faith in them at all. However, I am not here to criticize the packers any more than anyone else. I am certainly opposed to monopolies of all kinds; I have always been opposed to them. I say to-day the individual should get the chance to do business, but he is not getting it. The man with the best brains, the man who works the hardest, should be allowed to make some money. To-day you cannot make money unless you are a monopolist and have barrels of money. A few hundred thousand dollars is not enough; men with millions of dollars come along and drive you out of business. That is what is happening to-day in Toronto and Montreal. Hon. gentleman do not realize just how bad things are in the business world. I am not going to cry blue ruin, but just watch what may happen in the near future.

I take no objection to the hon. member for Parkdale not desiring to answer a question, Mr. Chairman. In fact I am in agreement with him in regard to the erection of an abattoir at the Atlantic coast. I think it would be an expensive experiment at the present time. I rose to point out that I think there was a period in the history of the Toronto civic abattoir when, under efficient management and without interference from the city hall, that abattoir operated successfully and showed a profit.
It always lost money.
Will the hon. member just do as he requested me to do when I asked him a question-kindly sit down and let me finish?
I shall keep quiet.

I am also in agreement with the idea that to a large extent we have a meat monopoly in the Dominion of Canada, and I do not think any monopoly operates to the best advantage of the majority of the citizens of this country.

Mr. Chairman, it has
been interesting to listen to the discussion this evening. I must say that I am not wholly in agreement with the hon. member for Parkdale, and I do not like to disagree with him, because I am generally in accord with his views.
The hon. member wants to be spoon-fed all the time.

Well, certainly I do not agree when he says that he was always done by the farmers. I do not think the farmers intend to do anybody. I believe if a census of the honest people of Canada were taken, you would find as many honest farmers as you would find honest men in any other line of business.
I did not say anything to the contrary.

It was interesting to hear the minister give the results of the trial shipments of fresh beef, and I certainly commend the department for what it is endeavouring to do in the way of shipping fresh beef to Great Britain. I would support many of the suggestions of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. The figures quoted tonight in regard to the shipment of live animals show that there has been no continuity in these shipments, with a very great differential between the high and low marks. For instance, in 1934 there were some 53,000 animals shipped. In 1935 that dropped to about 6,700. Then in 1936 it went up to 38,000, while in 1937 it was back to 9,000. It is quite apparent that you cannot have a market of any real value when there is such a fluctuation from one year to another, and I agree with the minister that it is quite proper to endeavour to develop a market for chilled or dressed beef. We might keep our shipments of live cattle to an average number, maintaining continuity in that respect, and then I think we could find a vast market for our dressed and chilled meat.
I want to refer briefly to dressed poultry. Saskatchewan is noted not only for its wheat and beef but also for its poultry I would
Supply-Agriculture-M arketing

remind hon. members of this committee- and no doubt the record can be found in the Department of Agriculture-that under the former Minister of Agriculture, Hon. Mr. Weir, a trial shipment of dressed poultry was sent to Great Britain, I think in the fall of 1931. That shipment, which consisted of some 800,000 pounds of dressed poultry, principally turkeys, was accompanied by an official of the department. I believe at least 80 per cent of that shipment came from the province of Saskatchewan. The poultry was dressed under the instructions of the officials of the department, and according to the report that came back the shipment was well received. The Saskatchewan birds found a ready market, and compared favourably with the home grown birds. I wish the minister would pursue some experiments, make some further trial shipments, with respect to poultry.
I might also remind the committee that in 1931, owing to the efforts of the government of that day and particularly of the Department of Agriculture, the embargo on cattle entering Great Britain was removed or the time within which they had to be slaughtered was extended. At that time I believe the live animals were permitted to enter and go to feed lots or to pasture. I think the records can be found in the department showing that a trial shipment was made of two carloads of cattle, one of which I think was of the Poll-Angus breed. One carload went to the feed lots and the other carload turned out to pasture, and the result was extremely favourable. Apparently the grass cattle took to the pasture over there readily and made wonderful gains, and that was also the case with the feed lots. That would open up a market for a different quality or weight of animal, and I understand if the right type and grade of live animal is shipped, a market might be developed for that lighter weight animal. Those are matters in connection with which the Department of Agriculture should be commended. There is a great market over there, and I trust the minister will bend every effort towards making further trial shipments and further experiments with respect to this matter.

What have been the results of shipments to Great Britain? Are thev living up to the trial shipments so far as quality is concerned, and how were those shipments received?

Yes; the quality is improving as they go along and as they obtain more experience. When I was overseas two years ago I found that the main criticism with respect to our poultry was not as to quality but as to the fact that it was not standardized. When the British retailer buys a box containing two or three dozen chickens he wants to know how much each will weigh when he takes it out of the box. Those chickens are sold to families of a certain size which require birds weighing a certain amount. The main criticism with our production was that while our poultry would come over in even better condition than the poultry from central European countries, it did not sell as well, because when the box was opened the merchant never knew what the size of the chicken was going to be. On the other hand, the chickens coming from central Europe were of uniform weight, and the weights were marked on the ends of the boxes. That seemed to be the main criticism, and we are attempting to overcome it by trying to improve our own packing. Grading has been developed along the same lines as the grading in connection with other products, and is gradually improving.
Was there any way by which the people could tell from what part of Canada the different shipments came?

In view of the fact that the quota to Great Britain has not been filled, can the minister say why the hog population of Canada decreased in 1937?

I have not the figures for 1937, but I am informed there was no decrease in the number in that year. On the contrary, there was a slight increase, although it may not have been as great as in previous years.
How many trial shipments of fresh eggs were sent to England in the last year?

In answer to the hon. member's former question the figures show that in 1935 the hog production amounted to 2,957,000; in 1936, to 3,796,000, and in 1937 to 3,966,000. It will be seen that there were about 170,000 more in the last year than in the previous year.

Would the minister answer my question as to how many trial shipments of fresh eggs were sent to Great Britain last year?
There has been a total export of a million and a quarter dozen. Four carloads were assembled in Montreal.
Were any trial shipments of fresh eggs made by the government last year?
The shipments are not made by the government. They are made by the packers, but the government assists in the assembling and grading of them.

In connection with the grading of hogs the minister said it was not compulsory to have hogs graded on the rail. If a farmer brings a load of hogs and the drover grades those hogs on foot, how must the drover sell them to the abattoir? Does the abattoir accept his-grading, or are they graded on rail by the abattoir?
The hogs are graded under government direction, and the packer accepts the grade given by the government inspector.

But where the drover buys hogs and grades them himself, on foot, will
the abattoir accept his grade when he sells them to that abattoir, or do they grade them on the rail?
I understand the abattoir accepts only the government grade.
Do I understand that they do accept the government grader's grade on foot?
The packer must accept the government grade.
According to the report of the committee which studied marketing in England, we find that each egg was labelled " empire." Is that still done, or has there been any amendment to -the regulation?

The regulation is in the old country, not here. I know, however, that they must be either graded with the name of the country from which they come, or marked " empire." Canadian eggs can be marked either way, but they must be marked one way or the other.
There is no regulation in the department stating they must be stamped with the word " Canada "?
If the regulations are applied to eggs, there will be, when the new regulations go into effect. But up to date there has not been any.
I know several shipments have been made from Napanee. As a matter of fact, fifty cases of fresh eggs were shipped last week to the old country and each egg had stamped upon it the word "Canada."
They would have to be stamped one way or the other.

The other evening we had some discussion about our shipments of bacon to the mother country. There is no doubt that this forms one of the most important items of export to Great Britain. The prices we receive in Great Britain do not compare very favourably with the prices received for bacon from Denmark and other countries. It has been said, I believe with a great deal of truth, that the prices received for our Wiltshire sides of bacon in the English market determine to a great extent the prices paid to the farmer in Canada. If we were receiving the same prices in England for our bacon as is received by Denmark and other countries, it would mean possibly a cent or more added to the price of hogs in Canada. Whether the difference would be as much as that, I do not know, but there is no doubt that there would be some difference, to the benefit of
Supply-A griculture-M arketing

the farmer. In the report known as the Shaw report there is a good deal of discussion about the type of bacon that goes to the mother country. I notice that under the heading, Selection and Grading, the following is said;
The grading and selection of Canadian bacon are not entirely satisfactory and must be improved. Selections are occasionally mixed, and, less frequently, grades are inaccurate.
The other night I made some reference to the fact that our bacon is not all inspected as it goes out for shipment to the old country; that there is simply a sample inspection. There are not too many abattoirs in Canada from which shipments of bacon, are made to the old country. We already have government graders and inspectors at the abattoirs, and I think it would be possible to see that the very best grade of bacon is baled. While I am on my feet I should like to refer further to this report. The statement is made that there are not enough Wiltshire sides shipped to the motherland, but that there are large quantities of what are known as box cuts and hams being sent to this market. The statement is made by the wholesalers over there that the large quantities of Canadian cuts have a depressing influence on the price of Canadian Wiltshires. It seems to me that something might be done, perhaps more than is being done now, to ensure that more Wiltshire sides of the proper size and grade are sent to the motherland. I have in my hand a pamphlet entitled, A Letter on Canadian Live Stock Products, dated February, 1938. Some reference is made to the size of bacon sent to the old country. There are three grades, and I understand within each grade there are three sizes. The standard grade runs between fifty-five and sixty-five pounds to the side. This is what is said in this letter:
In 1937, the bacon from Canada was exported in two grades, "A" and "B." Of the total shipped, 84 per cent was grade A and sixteen per cent was grade B. But only twenty-five per cent of the total export was of grade A sizeable. No. 1 selection, and sixteen per cent grade A sizeable, No. 2 selection.
The No. 1 selection is that which runs between fifty-five and sixty-five pounds. It goes on to say:
Considering the matter of weight alone, only 58 per cent of our bacon fell within the sizeable range of fifty-five to sixty-five pounds.
I cannot understand why that should be. This letter lays the blame largely at the door of the farmer, stating that he is marketing his hogs in sizes from which it is not possible to get this size of Wiltshire sides.
I believe there are sufficient hogs slaughtered in our abattoirs of select and bacon grades
(Mr. Senn.]
from which could be obtained sufficient of this size to fill all shipments. I wonder what is being done by the department to rectify this situation? So long as we continue to send undersize bacon and bacon of lower grades to England, we shall never realize the price for our bacon that other countries are getting. So long as we are getting a lower price than we should be, our farmers will not be realizing the prices they should. Just what is contemplated to remedy this situation?

There is a representative of the Department of Agriculture in London who checks this bacon as it comes over. It is quite true it is only a sample check as one man could not check it all. Where there is any reason for criticism, that criticism is sent back to the department and forwarded to whoever may be concerned. An attempt is made to have only the best quality shipped, and I think eventually that is what should be done. Only the best of our bacon should go to Great Britain. There is some question in the minds of those who wrote the report just referred to as to whether we can meet the demands which have been created by the development of that market up to the moment. However, an effort is being made to see that only the best goes forward.
What were our exports last year?

The minister says an effort
is being made, but what are the efforts?

In the first place, an effort must be made by the man who produces the hog. In the second place, an effort must be made by the man who feeds the hog. In the third place, an effort must be made by the man who houses the hog to see that it is housed properly. The only way to meet the competition of Denmark is to do what they do. The Danish people have a line of hogs which have been bred up to standard during the last 200 years. It is sometimes thought that the small shoulder and parts of the back having to do with the grading of the bacon are due altogether to the breeding, but I am informed that this is not the case. I am told that the manner in which the hog is housed has just as much to do with it as anything else. When a hog is allowed out to root around it develops a large neck, as people do who do other things, and it also develops a large shoulder. The Danish people stop the hog altogether from digging. They put him on cement where he can not work. All he does

Supply-Agriculture-Production
is eat the proper foods. The hogs have definite rations dealt out to them. When our hogs are let out to root up roots and other things they develop large shoulders and necks and all that kind of thing. It is absolutely impossible to get a standard slab of bacon with that kind of production. We shall have to start with the breeder and follow it through to the housing and feeding. We must get our people producing the one type in the one way all across Canada if we are to meet the competition of a country like Denmark.

I would not want the minister to leave the impression that the farmer is entirely to blame for this situation. I notice on page 958 of Hansard of this year an answer given by the minister to a question asked by the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor). The information is given that there were 714,847 hogs officially graded as selects in Canada in 1937. I do not know whether they have the heavy shoulders of which the minister speaks. If they had, I do not think they would be classed as selects. In addition, there were some 312,000 that were classed as A grade. In either one of these grades of hogs perfectly good Wiltshire sides can be obtained. There were only one million hogs shipped to England last year altogether, in the form of Wiltshire sides, so the minister's explanation that we are not shipping enough Wiltshire sides over there and laying the blame on the growers is not altogether warranted. I believe there is some difficulty within the packing industry itself, because no doubt they have to cater to the Canadian trade to a certain extent.
I thought that was what the hon. member advocated, that this was the trade to which we ought to cater.

Certainly, but we have also
a surplus that we must dispose of, and when the price we get in the British market determines the price which the farmer in Canada receives for his hogs, I do not think it is wise for us to send over bacon which is not going to command the highest price in the British market. If we cannot export a small quantity successfully, what are we going to do when we get a much larger hog population in this country? I am not particularly condemning the department. I am simply pointing this out to the committee because I believe there is something that can be done by way of inspection and supervision over the exports, and I am afraid that to-day this is left altogether too much in the hands of the packing industry itself, instead of having a supervision that might very well be undertaken by the department.

What is the number employed under this vote?
The details appear on page 59 of the estimates.
How jnany veterinary inspectors are employed?
The number is 262 veterinary inspectors this year as against 270 last year, and the complete service comprises 437 this year as against 447 last year.
Were any of these veteri-naries employed at the Carberry pasturage last year?

A few of them, in connection with the testing service. We tested all the breeding stock that passed through the pasture for Bang's disease and T.B., and there were veterinaries there carrying on that service.
Would the minister explain the great reduction in the compensation for animals slaughtered? I see it is less than half what it was last year.

Has the department any plan for eliminating Bang's disease in certain areas in a manner similar to the policy adopted for the eradication of tuberculosis in different areas? I know that certain resolutions have been passed by municipal councils and other organizations urging the government to adopt a policy similar to that which has been so successfully adopted for the elimination of tuberculosis.

We have not gone so far with this as we have gone with tuberculosis. As my hon. friend will recall, at the beginning of the activities in connection with tuberculosis there was considerable doubt whether the tests made were satisfactory and whether they were always reliable. We are experiencing exactly the same thing in connection with the Bang's. There is a great deal of disagreement at the moment as to whether the method followed to detect the disease and deal with it is satisfactory. Until that is fairly well established in the minds of breeders it is impossible to apply it in the same way. But we have, I understand, a number of herds that we are using at the present time in order to try to establish certain information, and consideration is being given to adopting certain areas and trying to clear Bang's disease out of those areas.
Where are the herds? I mean, are they in Ontario?
The herds are in the vicinity of Ottawa, by private arrangements with the owners. I was just questioning the advisability of naming the owners.
No; I am not asking that. I was asking if they are in Ontario.
Yes.

What investigational work is being done, if any, to ascertain just how far this disease has extended? From what I know of it, it seems to me that the ravages of the disease are more serious than even tuberculosis in its worst stage. There seems to be some hesitation on the part of those whose herds have the disease to let it be known, and I wonder if there is any investigational work going on to find out just how extensive this disease is. While 1 am on my feet, might I ask what work is being done by the department to develop new serums to eombat the disease and to provide a better

Supply-Agriculture-Health of Animals
method of testing for it. I understand that the province of Ontario, particularly through the college at Guelph, is doing quite an important work in this respect. Whether this department is cooperating with them or not, I do not know. I should like the minister to say what is being done both in the way of ascertaining the extent of the ravages of the disease and as to the reliability of the test, and to produce serums or some kind of inoculation that will do away with the disease.

The tests that we have conducted in connection with the first question, that is as to the extent to which the ravages of the disease are found, show about two per cent. Fifteen thousand have been checked, and out of the fifteen thousand we found two per cent. We checked all of the females that passed through Carberry pasture. They were gathered from a very large area in the western part of Canada, and that test showed 1-7 per cent, which is less than half of the reactors in tuberculosis, on an average, in the different areas. This would indicate that so far as investigation has gone the ravages of the disease are only about 50 per cent of what they are through tuberculosis. As to the reliability of the test, as I said a moment ago, that is something upon which all persons are not agreed. But I think the officials of the department are fairly well in agreement that the test which is being used is at least as satisfactory as can be expected.

What is being done in British Columbia in regard to Bang's disease? I think I drew to the attention of the minister last year that certain serums could be purchased across the line which veterinaries claimed were very effective, but they were not permitted to be brought into this country. Have they been investigated, looked into more thoroughly?

I understand that there has 'been some discussion with regard to calf vaccination with the hope of preventing the disease, but that is still in the experimental stage. We have about ten or twelve herds under observation at present in connection with the use of these serums. We are not yet in a position to state whether the serums are satisfactory or not.

There is a matter I discussed with the officials of this department a few days ago. A disease which is quite prevalent in certain parts of British Columbia is what is commonly known as red water, and I understand that the department about six years ago leased or took over a farm on the lower
mainland of British Columbia at which they were to carry on experiments. I believe they have demonstrated in the first place that the disease is not contagious, and also that it did not develop under certain conditions which were supposed to have caused its development. Of late it has been demonstrated, I believe, and the veterinary in charge is convinced, that it is more prevalent on what are known as rolling farms, where sloughs exist or similar conditions retain water for a certain length of time. What I want to impress upon the minister is the importance of carrying on that part of the investigation, at any rate of proceeding with it a little further. When I was at home at Easter I visited a number of farms, and it was suggested to me that on one of these farms a few acres might be leased-which could be done for fifty or sixty dollars a year-and some of the cattle taken from the farms located on the lower mainland, and placed on that land. The particular farmer's loss, I believe, runs to about twenty-seven cattle in the last ten or twelve years. Another farmer lost twenty-eight. One farmer I know of told me that his losses ran to somewhere about $200 or $250 a year. It is estimated that the total loss through this disease alone in the lower mainland will run to somewhere about $100,000 a year. The minister will, therefore, understand that it is quite important that this investigation should be pursued still further, and I trust that he will see fit to extend this research work in connection with the disease.

The research work in connection with the disease is being continued, and as has been suggested, every opportunity
is being taken of trying to meet the disease and find ways and means of preventing its development.
I notice that in the item of temporary assistance this year as compared with last there is an increase of approximately $80,000. Why is there such a large proposed increase in this item?

The increase in the temporary service is largely due to the fact that we have to set up organizations to take care of the inspections in connection with tuberculosis areas. The numbers vary from time to time, depending upon the amount of money that is voted by this committee for that purpose. If we get the amount we are asking for this year we shall do a certain amount of work, but if we are refused that amount we shall have to cut down on our staff. The supplementary estimates have not yet been considered, and

I cannot say what the extent of the work will be this year. Last year we obtained the amount we thought was necessary, and of course our temporary staffs throughout the country had to be increased to take care of the work. We do not put on permanent appointees to do all that work. The same applies to the inspection of meat. I would be glad to think that Bang's disease is prevalent only to the extent which the minister outlines, namely, two per cent of the cattle of the country. My impression was that it was much worse. What regulations are in effect for the shipment of cattle to the United States so far as Bang's disease is concerned? Is there any arrangement between the two countries? If so, what is it? I am under the impression that the regulations have been tightened up to some extent, and I believe they have also been tightened up with regard to cattle coming from the motherland. Can the minister give us any information?

The federal regulations for cattle going into the United States are the same as the regulations for cattle coming from the United States to Canada, but some of the states have regulations that differ from the federal regulations, and in those cases there may be greater difficulty in getting cattle into those states than there is in bringing cattle into Canada. The regulation is that breeding stock must be tested before it goes from Canada to the United States.
If they pass the test, are they accepted?
The federal government will accept them, but some of the states have additional requirements.
Have there been any changes recently in the regulations for cattle coming here or leaving the country?
There have been no recent changes so far as the federal governments are concerned.
What about cattle coming from England? I was under the impression that some changes had been made and that cattle that had been found free in England have now to be kept in quarantine.
Great Britain does not require a test for either Bang's or tuberculosis, but we do make the test. Cattle coming from Great Britain to Canada must submit to the test for Bang's and tuberculosis.

Is that in the motherland,
or after they come here? I believe that originally they could be tested in England, but now they have to be tested in quarantine here.

Yes; they are kept in
quarantine here.

How does
the minister arrive at the two per cent he mentioned?

That is, two per cent
of the 15,000 that we have tested. We do not know whether those herds may have been tested before and some weeded out. I should not like to say definitely, but I think the closest check so far as the west is concerned is the one made at Carberry where we gathered without selection every heifer or cow that came into the pasture, no matter where they came from, and checked them before they went out. That was less than two per cent, and it was a fair test of that particular area.

What number did that
cover?
Approximately 2,000.

The minister said that if the amounts asked for were not granted the number of inspectors would have to be reduced. I do not agree with those who believe that we have too many inspectors. In all our criticisms of the estimates so far it will be observed that very little has come from any part of the house with reference to the amounts expended or proposed to be expended. Personally I am sorry that the government sees fit to budget for only a little over $9,000,000 total expenditure in agriculture. I see no item in the estimates that looks too large, and in fact I would be glad to see the government take a more active part in connection with inspection generally, extending it until all the live stock of the dominion are covered. It is all the more important with reference to the export trade.
